papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while trying to retain their performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher output distributions to transferring internal representations or structured feature information, and from single-stage offline distillation to online and multi-teacher schemes. Empirical work across natural language, speech, vision and multimodal tasks shows that careful design—such as aligning intermediate features, adapting teachers to be student-friendly, using task- and domain-aware distillation, and leveraging online or instance-aware teacher weighting—can substantially reduce model size and latency with small performance loss. Still, distillation can introduce task-specific failure modes (e.g., degraded rare-word behavior or overfitting to teacher feature statistics), and practical deployment requires addressing teacher–student heterogeneity, data availability, and scalability.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for creating smaller, faster models from larger ones while retaining much of their functionality. When combined with representation matching, architecture-aware surgery, selective sample strategies, and privacy-aware protocols, KD enables deployment of high-quality models across modalities and constrained environments. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; without such care, distillation can underperform or transfer undesirable behaviors. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central, composable tool in compression toolkits, and outlines concrete methodological priorities that practitioners should follow to realize reliable, efficient distilled models.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies have become central tools to deploy large deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature shows diverse KD objectives (soft-label matching, representation matching, relational/correlation losses), architectural strategies (layer-wise, task-adaptive, student-friendly teacher training), data approaches (data augmentation, distilled or synthesized surrogates, zero-shot), and multi-teacher or ensemble-to-single compression. Empirical work across vision, generative models, reinforcement learning, and language tasks (including BERT compression and non-autoregressive translation) reveals consistent trade-offs between compression, accuracy, and robustness, and highlights practical constraints such as data heterogeneity and teacher-student capacity mismatch. Below we synthesize methods, observed benefits, limitations, and practical recommendations grounded in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical path to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A range of KD mechanisms—including soft-target supervision, intermediate feature or attention matching, multi-teacher fusion, data-free synthesis, and input-side augmentation—enable tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, privacy, and robustness. KD works best when its components are selected and adapted to deployment constraints: student capacity, available (or private) data, domain shift, and adversarial threats. However, important limitations remain, including distributional mismatch between teacher and student inputs, the preservation of robustness and fairness properties, and principled teacher selection. This article argues that a hybrid, constraint-aware KD strategy that combines representation-level transfer, data augmentation, and robustness- or privacy-aware synthesis offers the most reliable route to practical compression in real-world NLP and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Toolbox: Principles, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation should be understood and applied as a flexible set of techniques that go well beyond simple parameter compression. When treated as a toolbox—combining soft-target supervision, internal representation matching, layer-aware alignment, attention-guided mapping, and complementary compression methods—distillation can produce compact models that preserve accuracy, improve interpretability, and transfer robustness or privacy properties. Success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to prepare the student, and how to mitigate propagation of teacher defects; practitioners benefit from system-level designs that pair distillation objectives with pre-training, data augmentation, and architecture-aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Nuanced Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically proven approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. KD can operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure) and be combined with complementary compression techniques, data synthesis, or student-aware teacher training to meet deployment constraints in vision, language, and graph domains. However, its success depends on careful design choices — what to transfer, how to map teacher and student layers, how to handle limited or private data, and whether to adapt the teacher — and practitioners should treat KD as part of a broader compression toolkit rather than a universal solution.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Limitations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and richer internal signals. Techniques extend beyond matching teacher logits to include feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, adversarially-generated or adversarially-robust signals, online and multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. These methods enable deployment of compact models across vision and NLP tasks (including compressing pretrained transformers), improve efficiency on-device, and can sometimes preserve or even enhance robustness and generalization. Success depends on choices of distillation target, student architecture and capacity, the nature and availability of distillation data, and handling of domain or agent heterogeneity; open issues include transferring robustness reliably, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and principled handling of heterogeneous or private data sources.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and accelerates large neural models by transferring information from one or more teacher models into a smaller student. Across vision and language, KD variants extend from logit-matching to feature- and attention-level transfer, multi-teacher ensembling, online/co-distillation, privacy-aware and federated setups, and combinations with quantization or structured pruning. Practical pipelines combine KD with architecture-aware transformations, domain adaptation, and task-specific pretraining to obtain compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, or privacy constraints. Despite empirical success across modalities and deployment settings, trade-offs remain in teacher selection, information type to transfer, stability for heterogeneous architectures, and theoretical interpretation of what is transferred; these motivate further research into adaptive teacher weighting, feature alignment layers, and scalable privacy-preserving distillation for real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central approach to compress large deep models into smaller, faster student models suitable for resource-constrained deployment. A diverse set of strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and intermediate representation matching to multi-teacher ensembles, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-supervised or privacy-preserving protocols—have been developed to preserve accuracy, robustness, and modality transfer while reducing inference cost. Practical systems combine distillation with quantization, pruning, or architecture search to meet application-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other learned structure. Methods span data-dependent distillation using teacher soft targets and intermediate hints, multi-teacher and ensemble compression, many-to-many layer mapping for large pre-trained language models, data-free or zero-shot distillation where training data are unavailable, and approaches that combine distillation with quantization or pruning for deployment. Empirical results demonstrate that distillation can recover much of a teacher's accuracy while enabling efficiency gains, but trade-offs remain around robustness, optimization difficulty, domain shifts, and the need for careful alignment of inputs or representations. Recent work addresses these challenges with generative replay, adversarial objectives, layer-matching distances, and teacher-annealing strategies, yet open problems include theory of optimization, scalable privacy-preserving protocols, and balancing fairness or robustness with compression.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, multi-faceted approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Beyond simple teacher-student logits matching, distillation can be adapted to transfer inductive biases, deploy in federated or privacy-constrained settings, operate without access to original training data, and improve robustness and domain specialization. When combined with techniques such as feature mimicking, careful soft-label regularization, and online or ensemble-based training regimes, distillation provides a flexible toolkit to meet the efficiency, privacy, and deployment constraints of modern deep learning and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression and Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick but a core engineering technique that enables deployment, adaptation, privacy, and robustness for large neural models in real-world systems. By treating distillation as a family of methods—ranging from output soft-target transfer to feature- and layer-wise alignment, multi-teacher and online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols—practitioners can compress models while preserving task performance and satisfying latency, memory, and data-privacy constraints. Thoughtful application of KD, combined with complementary methods (pretraining, projector design, multi-stage schedules, and careful handling of teacher imperfections), yields compact models that are practical for production while exposing clear avenues for further research.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach to convert large, accurate models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what teacher signals to transfer, aligning mismatched architectures, and addressing data constraints—KD can preserve most teacher performance while enabling orders-of-magnitude improvements in latency, memory footprint, and deployability. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on representations transferred, the provenance and augmentation of distillation data, and deployment constraints such as privacy or distributed training. Effective compression therefore treats KD as a core tool within a broader toolkit that includes feature-level alignment, data-aware strategies, online or multi-teacher setups, and data-free techniques when real data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks, a consistent set of practices has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, intermediate-layer matching, and task- or domain-specific adaptation—augmented by variants that address missing data, distributed training, privacy, and teacher-student mismatch. Empirical results show that distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while enjoying large gains in inference speed and memory, and recent work clarifies when and why distillation acts as an effective regularizer.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, general-purpose approach for translating large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Across architectures, modalities, and deployment constraints, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher's performance; however, realizing those gains in practice requires matching the distillation formulation to data availability, model mismatch, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large models and transferring their capabilities to smaller or specialized models. KD can operate at multiple levels (logits, intermediate layers, and features), can be combined with model pruning and precision reduction, and can support domain adaptation and on-device deployment. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on how teacher knowledge is represented and transferred, the choice of data and augmentations used during distillation, and the deployment context (e.g., heterogeneous federated environments). When methods for intermediate-layer alignment, feature mimicking, data-side regularization, and architecture-aware mapping are combined thoughtfully, KD yields compact, efficient models that retain much of the teacher’s performance while enabling practical deployment in resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Adaptations, and Practical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but large neural models in resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models. Research has developed a spectrum of approaches — from matching logits to feature-level imitation, structural transformation of architectures, multi-teacher schemes, and task-specific adaptations — and has applied them across domains including detection, generative modeling, recommendation, retrieval, and multiple NLP tasks. Empirical work highlights both opportunities (substantial parameter reductions, faster inference, retained or modestly degraded accuracy) and pitfalls (propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to data heterogeneity, robustness concerns), motivating targeted algorithmic adjustments such as selective distillation, projector modules, and adversarially-aware distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger, higher-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other learned structure. Across NLP and broader deep-learning tasks, a family of techniques—logit/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, layer-wise mapping, multi-teacher and ensemble transfer, and data-free or generator-based synthesis—enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Distillation is both a practical engineering toolkit for deployment constraints (latency, memory, heterogeneity, privacy) and an active research area that raises challenges around preserving robustness, handling domain and data shifts, and designing principled curricula and teacher signals for maximal downstream utility.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Flexible — but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods have matured into a practical toolkit for producing smaller, faster models while retaining much of the performance of larger teachers. These techniques have been applied across domains (vision, speech, NLP, healthcare), settings (offline compression, federated learning, continual adaptation), and architectures (ensembles, transformers, detectors, GANs). However, their success depends on factors such as the availability and nature of data used for distillation, domain mismatch between teacher and student, robustness and privacy requirements, and optimization dynamics. KD can unlock high-performing compact models when combined with task-aware design choices (e.g., feature imitation, augmentations, architecture search, or ensemble teachers), but practitioners must account for trade-offs and failure modes to use it effectively.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool Beyond Simple Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be understood and applied as a flexible toolbox rather than merely a compression trick. KD enables compression, regularization, privacy-preserving transfer, and adaptation across diverse constraints (data scarcity, heterogeneous devices, federated settings). Effective practice combines soft-target supervision with representation-level alignment, architecture-aware methods (pruning, quantization, search), and privacy-aware or teacher-free variants. However, careful design is required to avoid capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors, and robustness or bias degradation.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Dependent Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while often preserving much of the teacher's effectiveness. KD methods range from matching soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations or using adversarial generators when training data are unavailable; they have been successfully applied across vision, generative modeling, recommender systems, and large pretrained language models. However, KD’s success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to address limited or private data, robustness, and bias—so practitioners must pair KD with task-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives to get reliable, deployable results.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Limited Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach that enables deploying large models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints by transferring knowledge from teacher to student models. KD extends beyond simple logit matching to include representation-level transfer, attention- and feature-guided objectives, multi-teacher schedules, and integration with architecture search and pretraining. While KD reliably improves efficiency and can preserve many teacher behaviors, its success depends on choices of distillation targets, teacher preparation, student architecture, and data strategies; it can also amplify teacher errors or struggle under data heterogeneity, requiring complementary techniques and careful engineering for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Practical Centrality and Conditional Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core engineering and research tool to compress large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across tasks and modalities show KD can substantially reduce parameter counts and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, and KD integrates naturally with complementary techniques (low-precision numerics, architecture search, pruning, federated or privacy-aware pipelines). At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey solution: optimization difficulties, imperfect teachers, data heterogeneity, privacy constraints, and robustness concerns require careful design choices and hybrid strategies. Effective deployment therefore depends on selecting which knowledge to transfer, adapting distillation signals to data and architecture mismatches, and combining KD with targeted algorithmic and system-level adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, Practical Benefits and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a simple teacher–student logit-matching trick into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large models and adapting their knowledge to resource- and data-constrained settings. Effective distillation operates at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational signals), interacts strongly with data and augmentation choices, and is most useful when combined with complementary compression methods and careful teacher–student design. While KD often yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance, its success depends on dealing with data availability, domain shift, teacher quality, and optimization dynamics—areas that remain active research directions.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or ensemble models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. It is used to reduce memory, compute, and latency for deployment, to enable low-precision inference, to protect privacy, and to adapt models across domains. Practical distillation methods vary in what is transferred (logits, features, relations), how teachers are chosen (single, multi-teacher, self), and how training is regularized (data augmentation, loss design, adversarial objectives). While distillation often yields students that outperform similarly sized models trained from scratch, mismatches between teacher and student, optimization difficulties, and domain/privacy constraints remain important concerns. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and language tasks shows that careful design choices (data augmentation, multi-stage distillation, private/noisy queries, and specialized losses) meaningfully affect student performance and deployment trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. Research over the past decade has produced a wide array of distillation variants (logit-based supervision, feature and attention matching, multi- and self-distillation, data-free methods) and shown how KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet practical constraints. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both the strengths of KD (regularization, practical deployment gains, domain adaptation) and its limits (optimization difficulty, capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors), motivating a pragmatic set of design choices for robust compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Callahan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, widely applicable strategy for compressing large neural networks into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation enables deployment of powerful pretrained models in resource-constrained settings, supports specialization (e.g., task or domain adaptation), and can be combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, pruning, architecture search) to produce practical, production-ready models. Advances in distillation methodology — including multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, teacher meta-learning, and task-aware layer-wise alignment — address fundamental challenges of capacity mismatch, information selection, and optimization stability, leading to more robust and efficient student models. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of any production-focused compression pipeline for deep learning and NLP systems, and that research emphasis on better teacher–student dynamics and task-aware transfer will yield the largest practical gains.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core of Model Compression: Effectiveness, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and NLP. When combined with complementary practices—task-aware signal selection, intermediate representation alignment, pretraining for compact architectures, multi-teacher or self-distillation, and data augmentation or synthesis—KD can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: data availability, teacher–student heterogeneity, fairness concerns, and theoretical gaps constrain its effectiveness in some settings. Careful design choices and hybrid pipelines are therefore required to realize reliable compression in production systems.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable faster, lower-memory, and more deployable systems. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD spans logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- and layer-wise matching, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, and architecture-aware strategies (e.g., progressive module replacement and projector layers). Effective compression depends on choices about what knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, how to treat data during distillation (augmentation, synthetic or few-shot settings), and whether teachers are trained to be student-friendly. When designed to match deployment constraints and task characteristics, distillation pipelines can preserve most teacher performance while improving inference speed, robustness, and sometimes calibration; but they also face failure modes including optimization difficulties, capacity mismatch, and distributional shifts that require targeted remedies.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are widely used to transfer predictive behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. A broad family of methods—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and layer-level mimicry, multi-teacher fusion, online and teacher-free protocols, and data-free or privacy-aware synthesis—has been developed and evaluated across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Empirical studies show that, when designed carefully (teacher selection, data strategy, and objective choice), KD can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling practical deployment; however, limitations remain around domain shift, robustness, preservation of fine-grained behaviors, and data- or architecture-mismatch, motivating hybrid strategies that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware training.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies aim to transfer predictive behavior from larger or more expensive models to smaller, faster, or more resource-efficient ones. The literature shows a variety of mechanisms (soft-label supervision, intermediate-feature alignment, progressive module replacement, adversarial feature matching), data- and training-focused interventions (data selection, augmentation, mixup, control of dataset complexity), and hybrid combinations with pruning or ensembling. Empirical results across NLP and vision tasks indicate that KD can preserve much of teacher performance while accelerating inference, but success depends strongly on (a) the choice of distillation targets and layer mappings, (b) the complexity and provenance of the distillation data, and (c) complementary techniques such as pre-training, feature-level matching, or structured pruning. Practical approaches therefore tailor the distillation recipe to model capacity, task characteristics, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ortiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, mature toolkit for turning large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Approaches vary from transferring softened outputs to aligning intermediate representations or relational structure, from online and multi-teacher schemes to data-free and privacy-aware pipelines. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and other modalities shows that well-designed distillation can preserve most of a teacher's performance while delivering substantial reductions in inference cost, parameter count, and memory footprint. Practical success depends on matching distillation targets and schedules to student capacity and deployment constraints, handling limited or private data appropriately, and addressing robustness, fairness, and distribution-shift concerns.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. Across vision and NLP, effective distillation combines choices about what to transfer (soft outputs, features, relational signals), how teachers are designed or ensembled, and what data or surrogates are used. Practical pipelines increasingly pair distillation with architecture search, curriculum strategies, and distributed training to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. While distillation often recovers much of a teacher's performance, success depends on careful alignment of objectives, data complexity, and optimization procedures; open problems include principled handling of imperfect teachers, robustness and fairness under compression, and scalable privacy-preserving distillation.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single training trick into a flexible, task-aware toolkit for compressing large models into efficient students suitable for real-world deployment. KD can transfer output behavior, internal representations, and relational or structural knowledge; it can be adapted to constraints such as missing training data, privacy, distributed training, and domain shifts; and when combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, pruning, task-aware layer selection) it produces compact models that retain much of the teacher's accuracy while meeting latency, memory, and privacy requirements. Practical use of KD requires matching the distillation strategy to the application constraints (what to transfer, which data to use, and how to align heterogeneous architectures).

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from matching soft teacher outputs into a flexible toolkit for producing compact, efficient models across vision and language. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can transfer final predictions, intermediate representations, relational structure, and inductive biases from large teachers to smaller students, and it is often most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when adapted to data constraints (real-data, augmented, or data-free regimes). Practical success depends on choices about distillation targets, teacher-student alignment, and data; remaining challenges include teacher imperfections, distributional mismatch, and preserving robustness and fairness under compression.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or multi-modal deep models into smaller, more deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or other structured knowledge. Work across vision, speech, and NLP shows a range of mechanisms (soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, layer mapping, and feature/attention guidance) and adaptations for limited or private data. Empirical results indicate distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while greatly reducing size and inference cost, but effectiveness depends on what knowledge is distilled, how it is represented, and the training regime.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transform large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or more private students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structured signals. Over the past decade these methods have evolved from logits-based soft-label transfer to a wide range of strategies including feature- and attention-matching, layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, data-free and privacy-preserving protocols, and adaptations for few-shot or federated settings. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation pipelines can retain much of teacher performance while substantially reducing model size and inference cost; however, effectiveness depends on what is distilled, student capacity, data availability, and practical constraints such as privacy, communication, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language, KD variants — from simple soft-target matching to feature-level, layer-aware, and many-to-many mapping approaches — enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to map layers, how to use or synthesize data, and whether to adapt teachers or students; remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous data and devices, preserving robustness and fairness, and enabling data-free or privacy-conscious distillation.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Leonard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compression, Generalization, and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a multifaceted technique that both compresses large models for efficient deployment and provides regularizing, transfer, and adaptation benefits beyond simple model-size reduction. KD can be integrated with architectural compression, multi-teacher training, and modality transfer to produce compact models that retain or even improve task performance while enabling deployment on heterogeneous devices and privacy-sensitive settings. However, KD is not a silver bullet: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and distilled-data artifacts can harm downstream behavior, so careful protocol design (multi-teacher aggregation, mixing hard labels, data-aware schemes, or data-free metadata approaches) and attention to internal-representation alignment are necessary to realize KD’s full potential.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Adaptations, and Practical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but large neural models in resource-constrained settings by transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models. Research has developed a spectrum of approaches — from matching logits to feature-level imitation, structural transformation of architectures, multi-teacher schemes, and task-specific adaptations — and has applied them across domains including detection, generative modeling, recommendation, retrieval, and multiple NLP tasks. Empirical work highlights both opportunities (substantial parameter reductions, faster inference, retained or modestly degraded accuracy) and pitfalls (propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to data heterogeneity, robustness concerns), motivating targeted algorithmic adjustments such as selective distillation, projector modules, and adversarially-aware distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression across Modalities and Deployment Constraints
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from a teacher to a student, KD can preserve accuracy while reducing model size and inference cost. Combining KD with task-aware objectives, data-augmentation strategies, and data-free synthesis techniques further extends its applicability to settings with limited task data, privacy constraints, or strict latency requirements. This paper argues that a principled, hybrid KD approach—tailored to the modality and deployment constraints—offers the best path to deployable, high-quality compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Limited Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach that enables deploying large models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints by transferring knowledge from teacher to student models. KD extends beyond simple logit matching to include representation-level transfer, attention- and feature-guided objectives, multi-teacher schedules, and integration with architecture search and pretraining. While KD reliably improves efficiency and can preserve many teacher behaviors, its success depends on choices of distillation targets, teacher preparation, student architecture, and data strategies; it can also amplify teacher errors or struggle under data heterogeneity, requiring complementary techniques and careful engineering for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Remaining Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, flexible strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in parameters and latency, and it generalizes across settings from data-poor or privacy-sensitive deployments to multi-teacher and online training regimes. However, practical success depends on careful choice of what to transfer (logits, features, relations), handling limited or absent training data, mitigating transferred biases, and aligning teacher-student architectures. I argue that KD should be the primary tool in production compression pipelines but must be combined with data synthesis, teacher selection/calibration, and fairness-aware design to realize robust, reliable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Composable Toolkit for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a composable toolkit—combining soft-target transfer, representation-level matching, data augmentation, selective sample strategies, and multi-teacher or federated adaptations—KD can produce efficient models that preserve much of teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. However, KD has known failure modes (teacher error propagation, data- and device-heterogeneity, and sample-wise regularization effects) that require explicit remedies and system-level design choices to ensure robust transfer.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation in NLP: Pre-training, Task-Awareness, Privacy, and Robustness
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large language models into smaller, faster students for NLP applications. Its effectiveness depends not only on the student-teacher framework but on complementary practices: pre-training compact models, aligning distilled signals to task-relevant representations, handling limited or private data, leveraging multiple teachers when available, and explicitly distilling for robustness. When these elements are combined and tuned, distillation yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints.
