papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language, KD variants — from simple soft-target matching to feature-level, layer-aware, and many-to-many mapping approaches — enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to map layers, how to use or synthesize data, and whether to adapt teachers or students; remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous data and devices, preserving robustness and fairness, and enabling data-free or privacy-conscious distillation.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Multifaceted Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a single training trick but a central, practical framework for compressing large models into deployable students. When treated as a toolbox—combining soft-label transfer, representation-level alignment, data augmentation or synthesis, and integration with other compression methods—KD enables substantial reductions in memory and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. However, realizing those gains requires deliberate design: choosing which teacher signals to transfer, addressing optimization and capacity mismatches, and using data-aware or data-free strategies when original training data are unavailable. I argue that KD should be the core component of any production-focused compression pipeline, paired with representation-level objectives and careful data strategies to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of large deep models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students, combining approaches such as soft‑label supervision, layer-wise or representation matching, and architectural reduction (pruning, layer skipping, parameter sharing). Research has extended distillation beyond supervised classification to domains including language models, sequence tasks, generative models, federated settings, domain adaptation, and few-shot or data-scarce regimes. Key practical challenges include maintaining accuracy under dataset or domain shift, training without access to original data, handling heterogeneous compute across devices, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and improving training efficiency. Effective solutions mix algorithmic choices (loss design, example selection, curriculum), data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or distilled data), and system-level integrations (joint optimization with pruning or layer removal).

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Necessity for Deploying Large NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Beyond simple logit matching, modern distillation encompasses feature-level mimicry, teacher adaptation, task-adaptive compression, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and continual or online schemes to maintain performance over time or across domains. When applied thoughtfully—choosing appropriate teacher signals, intermediate-target losses, and deployment-aware architecture search—KD enables real-world use of large pretrained models in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. Beyond the classic teacher-logit supervision, modern distillation covers feature-level matching, task-adaptive architecture search, multi-teacher transfer, and data-free scenarios. KD can be combined with pruning and structured sparsity, adapted for domain shifts, and used to transfer ensemble or task-specific knowledge into compact models. The choice of distillation target, the availability of data, and the deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, domain) determine which distillation recipe will be most effective.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. It is a practical toolkit used to reduce memory, compute, and latency for deployment, to enable low-precision inference, to adapt models across domains, and to support privacy-aware or federated settings. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and language tasks shows that careful choices about what to transfer, how teachers are configured, and how training is regularized materially affect the trade-offs between efficiency and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Efficient, Private, and Flexible Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks — from NLP to vision, speech, generative modeling, and graphs — KD enables deployment of high-quality models on resource-constrained devices. However, achieving reliable distillation requires attention to data availability, what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, or structural relationships), teacher design (multi-teacher and adaptive teachers), and constraints like privacy and fairness. When these factors are addressed, KD yields compact models that meet production constraints without wholesale loss of utility.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of practical and theoretical approaches for shrinking deep models while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, layer- and feature-level matching, architecture-aware transformations, teacher improvement or selection strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving pipelines, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-transfer applications, recent work shows that careful design choices—such as how layers are matched, which features to transfer, whether the teacher is static or trained to teach, and how to handle limited or private data—substantially affect the student’s final accuracy and deployment efficiency.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Practical Centrality and Conditional Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core engineering and research tool to compress large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across tasks and modalities show KD can substantially reduce parameter counts and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, and KD integrates naturally with complementary techniques (low-precision numerics, architecture search, pruning, federated or privacy-aware pipelines). At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey solution: optimization difficulties, imperfect teachers, data heterogeneity, privacy constraints, and robustness concerns require careful design choices and hybrid strategies. Effective deployment therefore depends on selecting which knowledge to transfer, adapting distillation signals to data and architecture mismatches, and combining KD with targeted algorithmic and system-level adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Pre-training Plus Strategic Distillation: Practical Principles for Compressing Deep NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are most effective when combined with deliberate choices about pre-training, the form of knowledge transferred, data manipulation during distillation, and adaptive teacher-student dynamics. Compact models that are pre-trained, trained to mimic both outputs and internal representations, and exposed to carefully designed augmented or mixed inputs can match much of the performance of larger models while meeting deployment constraints. However, compression success depends critically on optimization, data distribution, and task-specific phenomena such as rare-word behavior in sequence generation. I argue that a pragmatic pipeline—pre-train compact architectures, distill soft targets and internal representations, use augmentation/mixing to shape training data complexity, and apply adaptive or meta-learned teacher strategies—offers the best trade-off between efficiency and accuracy for deep learning and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Limited Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach that enables deploying large models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints by transferring knowledge from teacher to student models. KD extends beyond simple logit matching to include representation-level transfer, attention- and feature-guided objectives, multi-teacher schedules, and integration with architecture search and pretraining. While KD reliably improves efficiency and can preserve many teacher behaviors, its success depends on choices of distillation targets, teacher preparation, student architecture, and data strategies; it can also amplify teacher errors or struggle under data heterogeneity, requiring complementary techniques and careful engineering for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Practical, Task-Aware, and Privacy-Conscious Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical suite of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment across modalities and tasks. Effective KD goes beyond naive logits matching: task-aware layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher schedules, and architecture-aware search can preserve accuracy while reducing compute and memory. Moreover, self-distillation and teacher-free variants reduce dependence on strong teachers, and specialized KD variants address scarce data, privacy, and federated constraints. These directions together form a roadmap for applying KD in real-world deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Pham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical set of techniques to transfer predictive and representational knowledge from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across computer vision, generative modeling, retrieval, and natural language processing, practitioners use KD to reduce inference cost, enable on-device deployment, and adapt models to new domains or privacy constraints. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps), how teacher and student are aligned (layer mapping, attention-weighted projection, task-aware filters), and whether original training data are available (data-free and zero-shot approaches). Success depends on careful choices of teacher preparation, student capacity and architecture, signal selection, and data or synthetic-sample strategies; when designed appropriately, KD combined with complementary compression (pruning, architecture transforms) yields compact models with strong empirical performance, while important limitations remain (representation mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, low-frequency token coverage).

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Maddox
papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Nuanced Path to Model Compression in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques to transfer knowledge from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. When combined with complementary strategies — such as pre-training compact architectures, data augmentation, selective sample transfer, and module-level compression — KD can yield compact models that retain much of the teacher's utility. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on what is transferred, the availability and nature of data, teacher–student design, and optimization choices. Responsible deployment requires understanding both the practical strengths (efficiency, adaptability, applicability to privacy settings) and the limitations (data dependence, optimization gaps, possible degradation on rare or shifted inputs) of distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Galvan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, efficient students that retain much of the teacher's utility. KD operates through multiple mechanisms — transferring softened outputs, mimicking intermediate representations, and conveying relational or structural information — and is effective across vision and language tasks when adapted to task constraints. Practical deployment requires choosing what to distill, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited or unavailable training data, privacy, and fairness concerns. When combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, pruning) and task-aware curricula or sample selection, KD enables reliable, efficient models for resource-constrained applications while exposing important open research questions around robustness, optimization, and equitable behavior.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while attempting to retain performance. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD variants address constraints such as limited computation, on-device heterogeneity, lack of access to teacher training data, fairness concerns, and the need for task-specific efficiency. Common themes include transferring softened output distributions, matching intermediate representations, using multiple teachers or self-generated targets, and integrating compression with architecture search or pre-training. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact, practical models for deployment, but also reveals optimization and data-dependence limitations that motivate method refinements like task-adaptive search, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, and self-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and empirically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and deployment constraints, KD enables moving from research-stage, high-capacity architectures to resource-efficient models suitable for latency- and privacy-constrained production. Realizing KD's full potential requires attention to teacher quality, data and domain mismatches, and scalability; appropriate choices—representation-level objectives, multi-teacher signals, online protocols, and privacy-aware distillation—address these challenges and make KD a core tool for applied deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks, a consistent set of practices has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, intermediate-layer matching, and task- or domain-specific adaptation—augmented by variants that address missing data, distributed training, privacy, and teacher-student mismatch. Empirical results show that distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while enjoying large gains in inference speed and memory, and recent work clarifies when and why distillation acts as an effective regularizer.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Conditional Endorsement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are indispensable tools for deploying high-capacity deep models in resource- and latency-constrained settings. When combined with architecture-aware strategies, task adaptation, and data-aware protocols, KD recovers much of teacher performance while enabling substantial speed and size reductions. However, distillation is not a universal remedy: optimization difficulties, domain and low-frequency token mismatches, privacy or data-availability constraints, and fairness concerns require tailored remedies. Effective compression thus integrates KD with architecture search, progressive replacement, data-free methods, and fairness- and federated-aware training to achieve reliable, deployable students.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Versatile Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable compression paradigm that transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller students. When carefully applied, KD enables deployment of performant, efficient models across tasks and modalities, addressing constraints such as inference cost, memory, data availability, and privacy. However, effectiveness depends on what is distilled (outputs vs. internal representations), the availability of training data, and training dynamics; understanding these aspects guides practical decisions that combine KD with quantization, architecture design, and training curricula to produce reliable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Design-Sensitive Path to Compact Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation offers a practical route to compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students that retain much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness arises from multiple distillation signals (soft labels, intermediate representations, attention or channel maps) and from combining distillation with pre-training, architecture-aware design, and data-management strategies. However, realizing these gains in real systems requires explicit choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited, private or heterogeneous data.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring useful predictive behavior and representations from a teacher to a student. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, adversarial or data-free approaches, and online or federated variants that trade communication and privacy constraints against fidelity. Practical success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to manage imperfect or heterogeneous data and devices, and whether to combine distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., pruning or architecture search). While distilled students often retain much of a teacher's performance and enable deployment under latency or resource constraints, open challenges include preserving rare-token behaviors, handling domain shift and robustness, and designing privacy- and communication-efficient protocols for real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Paradigm for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a compression trick: when treated as a broad training paradigm it enables compact, robust, and deployable models across modalities and tasks. By integrating logit-level guidance, intermediate feature transfer, architecture-aware projectors, adaptive teacher selection, data- and domain-aware strategies, and robustness-aware objectives, KD pipelines can produce students that approach teacher performance while satisfying latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Practical success requires designing what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous components, and how to shape inputs and curricula for the student—rather than relying on a single generic distillation recipe.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are widely used to transfer behavior from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling deployment under resource constraints. Research over the past decade has developed variants that target outputs (soft labels), internal representations (layer-wise and attention-based methods), data regimes (data-free or distilled training sets), and architecture search for task-aware compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the practical gains and fundamental limits of distillation, and points to best practices such as pre-training compact models, selecting or synthesizing appropriate training data, and aligning student capacity to distilled signal.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: Practical Knowledge Distillation for Deploying Large NLP and Deep Models: A Unified Argument for Multi-Teacher, Data-Agnostic, and Federated Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and essential set of techniques for compressing large deep and language models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. A mature KD strategy must simultaneously preserve teacher knowledge, generalize across domains and distributions, and respect deployment constraints (e.g., lack of original data or heterogeneous client devices). Empirical and methodological advances show that combining multi-teacher strategies, data-agnostic/distillation-from-generator approaches, feature-level projectors or ensembles, targeted augmentation, and adaptations for federated settings yields robust, efficient student models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a System: Practical Strengths, Limits, and Prescriptions for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a modular system—combining soft-target supervision, representation-level objectives, data augmentation, multi-teacher signals, and complementary compression methods—KD reliably yields compact models that preserve much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. Effectiveness depends on handling data availability, architecture mismatches, and undesirable teacher artifacts; these constraints are manageable when KD is designed with domain adaptation, input alignment, and augmentation-aware strategies. I argue KD should be the default toolchain for producing production-ready compact models, applied with explicit attention to what knowledge is transferred and how it is matched to student capacity and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable transfer of predictive power from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The literature has expanded beyond soft-label matching to include internal-representation distillation, module replacement, self-distillation, selective sample transfer, and adaptations for constraints such as privacy, communication, and low-precision inference. Applied across domains—from NLP rankers and translation to graph, vision-language, and speech systems—these methods trade off fidelity, efficiency, and robustness through a variety of algorithmic and engineering solutions.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Riley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying high-performing deep models under resource constraints. Methods range from transferring soft-output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, many-to-many layer mappings, and task- or domain-adaptive compression of large pretrained language models. Advances address practical concerns such as absence of original data, low-precision inference, cross-modal transfer, and faster training-time distillation workflows. Empirical work demonstrates that representation-level supervision and flexible layer alignment often outperform pure logit-based approaches, while theoretical analyses connect KD to regularization schemes like label smoothing and quantify when teacher signals are most beneficial. Remaining challenges include preserving rare-token behaviors, handling domain shift, and balancing privacy, compute, and accuracy in on-device scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient students suitable for deployment. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Success depends on choosing appropriate distillation strategies that account for model structure, task specificity, data availability, and training dynamics. When tailored—via structural transformations, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer alignment, or data-centric augmentations—distillation consistently produces compact models that approach teacher accuracy and enable real-world use cases that would otherwise be impractical.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in NLP: Capabilities, Extensions, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep learning models for NLP and related domains. When combined with complementary strategies—pretraining of compact models, layer-matching techniques, targeted data augmentation, robustness-aware objectives, privacy-aware protocols, and adaptive teacher training—distillation can produce small models that retain much of the teacher's accuracy while meeting deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and intermediate representations. Across vision, speech, and language tasks KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while often preserving most of the teacher’s performance. Practical use of KD involves choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention), how to handle data mismatches (data augmentation, synthetic data, or data-free methods), and how to combine distillation with complementary techniques (pretraining, pruning, quantization, federated protocols). Despite broad empirical success, open problems remain in preserving low-frequency behaviors, robustness and fairness, and in designing principled curricula and teacher-student interfaces for diverse deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are mature, diverse strategies to reduce the computational and memory costs of large deep models while retaining much of their task performance. Approaches span architecture-level methods that search or prune for compact student networks, training-time methods that transfer dark knowledge via logits or intermediate representations, and data-centric methods that operate when original training data are unavailable. Empirical work shows success compressing large language models into lightweight networks for NLP tasks, highlights task- and data-specific pitfalls (notably for low-frequency tokens in sequence tasks), and motivates specialized extensions in federated and domain-adaptive settings. Theory and interpretive analyses have begun to clarify why distillation helps generalization and optimization, and recent work advocates shaping teachers to be more student-friendly or designing student-aware compression procedures. Overall, the literature shows a practical toolkit of complementary techniques—task-adaptive architecture search, feature- and attention-based matching, adversarial or synthetic-data distillation, and teacher-student co-training—each with trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to teacher behavior.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.
