papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks, a consistent set of practices has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, intermediate-layer matching, and task- or domain-specific adaptation—augmented by variants that address missing data, distributed training, privacy, and teacher-student mismatch. Empirical results show that distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while enjoying large gains in inference speed and memory, and recent work clarifies when and why distillation acts as an effective regularizer.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Not Sufficient Tool for Compression and Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling substantial runtime, memory, and latency gains while preserving much of predictive performance. KD is effective across modalities and deployment regimes, but its success depends on careful method choice, teacher quality, data availability, and combination with complementary compression strategies. Future progress requires deeper theoretical understanding, better automation for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive settings, and principled integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in NLP and Deep Learning: Necessity, Challenges, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models and transferring desirable properties (accuracy, robustness, or representations) into smaller, deployable students. In NLP and related deep-learning domains, distillation enables the efficient use of pretrained teachers, supports domain adaptation and continual learning, and can be adapted for supervised, self-supervised, and adversarial objectives. However, naive distillation can degrade specific behaviors (e.g., lexical choices or uncertainty calibration) unless the distillation pipeline addresses alignment of inputs and representations, intermediate-layer supervision, the sample-wise effects of soft labels, and robustness transfer. I argue that distillation should be treated as a design problem—choosing which knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student representations, and when to expose students to raw or adversarial signals—to yield compact models that preserve both accuracy and desirable inductive properties.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role and Practical Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core set of techniques for converting large, expensive neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for real-world deployment. KD variants transfer soft outputs, intermediate representations, or structural behaviors; they can be combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture modification) and adapted for constrained data, privacy, and deployment regimes. However, distillation’s success depends on principled choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, how to obtain or synthesize training data, and how to mitigate teacher-induced errors or biases. Practical deployments therefore require task-aware distillation design, careful teacher selection or adaptation, and evaluation of failure modes such as degraded rare-token behavior or domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger, higher-capacity models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other learned structure. Across NLP and broader deep-learning tasks, a family of techniques—logit/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, layer-wise mapping, multi-teacher and ensemble transfer, and data-free or generator-based synthesis—enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Distillation is both a practical engineering toolkit for deployment constraints (latency, memory, heterogeneity, privacy) and an active research area that raises challenges around preserving robustness, handling domain and data shifts, and designing principled curricula and teacher signals for maximal downstream utility.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are central tools for converting large, high-performing deep models into smaller, faster models that are practical for deployment. A broad repertoire of methods exists—matching soft logits, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial and online co-training, and data- or task-aware augmentation—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical evidence shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, but success depends on how teacher signals are represented, what data are used, and how architecture or domain mismatches are addressed. Practical deployment requires attention to data availability, privacy or federated constraints, teacher errors, and optimization stability; promising directions include pre-training compact students, online and federated distillation protocols, and specialized layer- or modality-aware objectives.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical and Multifaceted Engine for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical set of techniques that enable deploying high-performing deep models under computation, memory, data, and privacy constraints. By transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure from large teachers to compact students, KD supports domain specialization, model acceleration, privacy-preserving release, and improved generalization. Best results come from matching the KD strategy to the constraints and goals of the application (e.g., multi-teacher aggregation, representation-level transfer, data-free generation, or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. While classic distillation focuses on matching teacher output probabilities, practical compression across modalities and tasks benefits from richer transfer mechanisms: aligning internal representations, selecting task-relevant signals, leveraging data augmentation or synthetic data when real data are scarce, and using adversarial or ensemble strategies to expose diverse and robust teacher knowledge. When combined thoughtfully these methods enable students that are much smaller and faster while retaining or even improving accuracy and robustness on downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core technique for producing compact, deployable neural models by transferring predictive behavior or internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller students. KD encompasses a spectrum of objectives — from matching soft output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, relational statistics, or task-specific features — and it is often combined with architectural modification, pruning, quantization, or data synthesis to meet deployment constraints. Practical KD addresses data scarcity, domain shift, heterogeneity of devices and architectures, and privacy concerns through strategies such as data-free distillation, multi-teacher weighting, teacher adaptation, and curriculum or instance-aware sampling. While KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss, careful design is needed to avoid capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, and degradation on rare or out-of-domain inputs.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression and Practical NLP Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teacher's effectiveness. A growing body of work shows KD's versatility across modalities (vision, speech, text), deployment regimes (edge devices, distributed training), and model families (transformers, convolutional nets, generative models). Combining richer teacher signals (intermediate representations, attention maps, or learned teacher updates), stronger input-side practices (data augmentation), and complementary compression methods (architecture search, pruning) yields robust, efficient students suitable for real-world constraints. This paper argues that distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit whose components are chosen to match task constraints, and it highlights promising techniques to improve transfer fidelity, training efficiency, and downstream performance.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Complementarities
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable deployment of large deep models by transferring knowledge from high-capacity teachers to smaller students or by combining compression methods. Work in this area spans practical recipe development for NLP and vision models, theoretical analyses of when and why distillation helps, methods that go beyond soft logits to internal feature transfer, strategies for multi-teacher and ensemble compression, approaches for data-limited or data-free settings, and complementary compression techniques such as pruning and quantization. Empirical results show that careful choices (e.g., which samples or layers to use, how to combine teachers, and how to map teacher-to-student layers) matter for final accuracy; theoretical results explain tradeoffs between soft and hard labels, and methods exist that make distillation feasible without teacher data or with constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Engine for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a heuristic into a set of principled, modality-agnostic techniques that enable deployment of high-capacity models in resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings. By transferring predictive behaviour and internal representations from large teachers to compact students, distillation preserves much of the teacher's utility while enabling large speed, memory, and communication gains. Recent advances show that combining representation-level matching, teacher–student co-design, data-free synthesis, and task-adaptive compression yields robust, practical pipelines for compressing models across vision, language, graph, and federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation unifies multiple strategies for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable models while preserving performance. It supports a range of goals — parameter and latency reduction, robustness, interpretability, and privacy-aware deployment — by transferring information from a teacher to a student via soft outputs, intermediate representations, or structural/architectural guidance. Practical and research advances show that combining distillation modes (feature-level, output-level, progressive module replacement), data augmentation, and adaptive teacher training yields compact models that approach teacher performance even under limited data, heterogeneous devices, or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structured relationships. Across deep learning and NLP, KD enables deployment of performant models under latency, memory, and privacy constraints and is routinely combined with complementary compression methods. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features), how to align teacher and student architectures, the availability and design of distillation data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and training protocols that mitigate capacity and distribution mismatches. Open challenges include robust teacher selection, data- and domain-mismatch, and scaling distillation methods to heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core of Model Compression: Effectiveness, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and NLP. When combined with complementary practices—task-aware signal selection, intermediate representation alignment, pretraining for compact architectures, multi-teacher or self-distillation, and data augmentation or synthesis—KD can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency and resource constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: data availability, teacher–student heterogeneity, fairness concerns, and theoretical gaps constrain its effectiveness in some settings. Careful design choices and hybrid pipelines are therefore required to realize reliable compression in production systems.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Toolbox: Principles, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation should be understood and applied as a flexible set of techniques that go well beyond simple parameter compression. When treated as a toolbox—combining soft-target supervision, internal representation matching, layer-aware alignment, attention-guided mapping, and complementary compression methods—distillation can produce compact models that preserve accuracy, improve interpretability, and transfer robustness or privacy properties. Success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to prepare the student, and how to mitigate propagation of teacher defects; practitioners benefit from system-level designs that pair distillation objectives with pre-training, data augmentation, and architecture-aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Practical, Task-Aware, and Privacy-Conscious Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical suite of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment across modalities and tasks. Effective KD goes beyond naive logits matching: task-aware layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher schedules, and architecture-aware search can preserve accuracy while reducing compute and memory. Moreover, self-distillation and teacher-free variants reduce dependence on strong teachers, and specialized KD variants address scarce data, privacy, and federated constraints. These directions together form a roadmap for applying KD in real-world deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central practical mechanism to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment in resource-, latency-, or privacy-constrained settings. Research has developed a family of distillation objectives (soft logits, feature/representation matching, relational/correlation losses), training schedules (multi-stage, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or distilled corpora, data-free queries) that, when combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), enable compact models to recover much of the original performance. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to map teacher and student representations, and how to adapt pretraining and task data to the student’s capacity; remaining challenges include domain shift, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency behavior in NLP, and privacy-aware distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Capabilities, Limitations, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and graph domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, speed up training at scale, and allow transfer of robustness or domain expertise when carefully designed. However, successful distillation depends on alignment of teacher and student inputs/representations, the choice of distilled signals (logits, features, attention, or contrastive embeddings), and careful handling of privacy, robustness, and domain shift. Best practice combines representation-level matching, adaptive teacher strategies, confidence-aware multi-teacher fusion, and privacy- or robustness-aware objectives to meet practical constraints while maximizing student performance.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or ensemble neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across computer vision, speech, multimodal, and NLP tasks, distillation protocols—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate feature and attention-based transfers—enable practical trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and memory. Success depends on careful choices of distillation targets, teacher-student compatibility, data availability, and training dynamics; when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, low-precision, architecture search, or federated protocols) it yields deployable models for resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Nuanced Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically proven approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. KD can operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure) and be combined with complementary compression techniques, data synthesis, or student-aware teacher training to meet deployment constraints in vision, language, and graph domains. However, its success depends on careful design choices — what to transfer, how to map teacher and student layers, how to handle limited or private data, and whether to adapt the teacher — and practitioners should treat KD as part of a broader compression toolkit rather than a universal solution.

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Versatile Toolbox: Principles, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation should be understood and applied as a flexible set of techniques that go well beyond simple parameter compression. When treated as a toolbox—combining soft-target supervision, internal representation matching, layer-aware alignment, attention-guided mapping, and complementary compression methods—distillation can produce compact models that preserve accuracy, improve interpretability, and transfer robustness or privacy properties. Success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to prepare the student, and how to mitigate propagation of teacher defects; practitioners benefit from system-level designs that pair distillation objectives with pre-training, data augmentation, and architecture-aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while attempting to retain performance. Across computer vision and natural language processing, KD variants address constraints such as limited computation, on-device heterogeneity, lack of access to teacher training data, fairness concerns, and the need for task-specific efficiency. Common themes include transferring softened output distributions, matching intermediate representations, using multiple teachers or self-generated targets, and integrating compression with architecture search or pre-training. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact, practical models for deployment, but also reveals optimization and data-dependence limitations that motivate method refinements like task-adaptive search, multi-teacher weighting, data-free synthesis, and self-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Contemporary Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. Across computer vision and natural language processing, a wide family of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, multi-teacher and online schemes, many-to-many layer mappings, and task-aware layer selection—has been developed to trade off accuracy, latency, and model size for practical deployment. Empirical work shows that combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware transformations) and adapting distillation signals to task and data constraints yields compact models that capture much of teacher performance. At the same time, distillation must contend with capacity mismatch, robustness and distribution-shift sensitivity, privacy concerns, and the need for principled layer- and signal-alignment strategies—areas that motivate continued methodological and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, general-purpose approach for translating large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Across architectures, modalities, and deployment constraints, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher's performance; however, realizing those gains in practice requires matching the distillation formulation to data availability, model mismatch, and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. The literature has expanded beyond soft-label matching to include intermediate representation imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and adaptive-teacher schemes, data- and domain-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning or architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can preserve a large fraction of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, while theoretical and empirical analyses clarify when distillation helps, how teacher quality and data regimes affect outcomes, and what practical trade-offs remain. Open problems center on robustness to domain shift and adversaries, distillation without original data, and automated, architecture-agnostic pipelines for production systems.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Not Sufficient Tool for Compression and Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling substantial runtime, memory, and latency gains while preserving much of predictive performance. KD is effective across modalities and deployment regimes, but its success depends on careful method choice, teacher quality, data availability, and combination with complementary compression strategies. Future progress requires deeper theoretical understanding, better automation for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive settings, and principled integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Practical, Private, and Robust Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is often framed narrowly as a model-compression trick to shrink large neural networks. This paper argues KD should instead be viewed as a core engineering and scientific tool for practical deployment: it enables training with limited or private data, yields task- and domain-adaptive compact models, improves robustness and fairness, and transfers intermediate representations and attention patterns that standard supervised training cannot. We synthesize evidence from recent work to show how variants of KD—self-distillation, layer-wise projection, multi-teacher schemes, teacher annealing, and data-free distillation—address concrete deployment challenges in vision and NLP, and we derive practical recommendations for combining these techniques in real systems.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques shrink large neural models into smaller, faster models for constrained deployment while attempting to preserve task performance. A diverse set of approaches—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or generative sample synthesis—has emerged across vision, language, multimodal, and graph tasks. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention maps, or structural priors), how to align heterogeneous architectures, whether teacher or student are adapted during training, and how to handle limited or absent training data. Empirical work shows substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost are possible with modest performance loss, but open problems remain around principled teacher selection, robustness under domain shift, privacy, and closing optimization/capacity gaps between teachers and students.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Necessity for Deploying Large NLP and Deep Learning Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Beyond simple logit matching, modern distillation encompasses feature-level mimicry, teacher adaptation, task-adaptive compression, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and continual or online schemes to maintain performance over time or across domains. When applied thoughtfully—choosing appropriate teacher signals, intermediate-target losses, and deployment-aware architecture search—KD enables real-world use of large pretrained models in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core practical approach for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while retaining much of the original performance. Multiple distillation mechanisms—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial/ensemble-based transfer, and data-free or selective-sample techniques—allow KD to address constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous deployment, low-precision hardware, and domain shift. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a transfer of representational structure and as a regularizer; its success depends on choices about what is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, how training data (real or synthetic) are used, and which complementary compression methods are applied. Remaining practical challenges include distributional mismatch, heterogeneity of architectures and devices, and principled teacher selection and optimization strategies.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations. Across modalities and tasks, distillation methods vary by what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate features, attention, or structural knowledge), by whether they rely on original training data, and by how the teacher-student relationship is optimized. Practical goals include reducing inference cost, preserving accuracy under domain shift, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, and improving robustness or fairness. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen transfer targets, training curricula, and data strategies can recover much of the teacher performance in compact models, and that meta-level and task-adaptive approaches further improve transfer effectiveness. Key open concerns are how to best align heterogeneous inputs or architectures, how to retain desirable inductive biases (e.g., for domain-specific tasks), and how to ensure reliable student performance without access to teacher training data.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient students suitable for deployment. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Success depends on choosing appropriate distillation strategies that account for model structure, task specificity, data availability, and training dynamics. When tailored—via structural transformations, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer alignment, or data-centric augmentations—distillation consistently produces compact models that approach teacher accuracy and enable real-world use cases that would otherwise be impractical.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD operates through multiple mechanisms—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, transferring relational structure, and providing regularization—that together enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. KD integrates naturally with other compression methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization), supports data-free and privacy-sensitive settings, and scales across modalities and deployment constraints. At the same time, effective distillation requires careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to map teacher and student layers, how to handle imperfect teachers and data mismatch, and when to combine KD with complementary techniques. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a toolbox rather than a single recipe and offers practical, evidence-based recommendations for deploying KD in real systems.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Best Practices and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable models across vision, language, and structured-data domains. KD works at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention, and structural guidance) and combines naturally with complementary methods—student pretraining, data augmentation or synthesis, multi-teacher and ensemble signals, architecture-aware losses, and privacy-aware generation—to produce compact models that retain much of the teacher’s utility while satisfying latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Effective deployment requires careful choices of distillation targets, alignment strategies, and data-handling procedures, and awareness of common failure modes (optimization instability, teacher error propagation, and domain/device heterogeneity).

papers_seen.author: Dixon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods compress large deep models into smaller, faster, or more private models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature shows a spectrum of KD signals (soft logits, intermediate features, layer mappings), enhancements via data interventions and architecture search, and combinations with pruning or low-precision inference. Practical success depends on task- and deployment-aware choices (which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, what augmentations or synthetic data to use) as well as attention to privacy and robustness. The field has produced effective recipes for compressing pretrained language models, vision transformers, and generative models, while ongoing work clarifies limits and complementary techniques for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies have become central tools to deploy large deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature shows diverse KD objectives (soft-label matching, representation matching, relational/correlation losses), architectural strategies (layer-wise, task-adaptive, student-friendly teacher training), data approaches (data augmentation, distilled or synthesized surrogates, zero-shot), and multi-teacher or ensemble-to-single compression. Empirical work across vision, generative models, reinforcement learning, and language tasks (including BERT compression and non-autoregressive translation) reveals consistent trade-offs between compression, accuracy, and robustness, and highlights practical constraints such as data heterogeneity and teacher-student capacity mismatch. Below we synthesize methods, observed benefits, limitations, and practical recommendations grounded in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking large deep models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable models while retaining much of their performance. Research has expanded beyond the original logit-based teacher-student paradigm to include feature mimicking, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, multi-teacher and adaptive-teacher strategies, and task- or hardware-aware compression. These methods have been applied across modalities — including vision, graphs, generative models, and a broad set of NLP tasks — and are increasingly combined with architecture search and pruning to meet deployment constraints. Despite empirical successes, important questions remain about what knowledge is most useful to transfer, how to select or adapt teachers, and how to operate under data, compute, or privacy limitations.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Paradigm for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated not as a narrow compression trick but as a unifying, practical paradigm for producing compact, deployable models while preserving accuracy, robustness, and task-specific behavior. KD’s range—spanning soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and adversarial or curriculum-enhanced transfers—makes it uniquely suited to combine with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet real-world constraints. At the same time, KD requires careful design to handle teacher-student mismatch, low-frequency phenomena, domain shift, and data-availability or privacy limits; following representation-aware objectives, adaptive teacher strategies, and hybrid compression pipelines yields the most reliable results.

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical but Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones. When used thoughtfully, KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on which signals are transferred (logits, features, relational information), alignment between teacher and student, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and awareness of teacher imperfections. Combining KD with representation-level matching, task-aware layer alignment, online or federated protocols, and data strategies yields the best trade-offs for real systems.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: The Case for Practical, Adaptive Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible tool for compressing large deep learning models into deployable students. Recent work shows KD can both directly reduce model size and serve as a mechanism to transfer inductive biases, intermediate representations, and task-specific attention. However, real-world constraints — limited or private training data, domain and client heterogeneity, and redundant teacher representations — require KD methods that are data-free, adversarially robust, task-aware, and selective about what teacher knowledge to transfer.
