papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Practical, Private, and Robust Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is often framed narrowly as a model-compression trick to shrink large neural networks. This paper argues KD should instead be viewed as a core engineering and scientific tool for practical deployment: it enables training with limited or private data, yields task- and domain-adaptive compact models, improves robustness and fairness, and transfers intermediate representations and attention patterns that standard supervised training cannot. We synthesize evidence from recent work to show how variants of KD—self-distillation, layer-wise projection, multi-teacher schemes, teacher annealing, and data-free distillation—address concrete deployment challenges in vision and NLP, and we derive practical recommendations for combining these techniques in real systems.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Roles, Limits, and Best Practices for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly framed as a route to compress large models into smaller deployable students, but its benefits and pitfalls extend well beyond mere parameter reduction. KD acts as a form of learned regularization, can be applied in self-distillation and teacher-free regimes, and enables transferring properties such as robustness, privacy-preserving signals, and task-specific intermediate knowledge. At the same time, KD faces optimization and representation-mismatch challenges and can propagate undesirable biases from teacher to student. This paper argues that practitioners should treat KD as a flexible toolbox: combine soft-label supervision with internal-representation matching, flexible layer-mapping, attention-guided feature alignment, and targeted interventions for fairness, privacy, and robustness to get consistent benefits in both vision and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a set of teacher→student techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving students. Across vision and NLP, KD variants include soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and feature-level imitation, relational or structure-preserving losses, multi-teacher ensembles, data-agnostic or data-free procedures, and self- or cross-supervised transfer. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing compact models but requires careful handling of data regimes, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and robustness or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster models while preserving— and in some settings improving—accuracy, robustness, and domain suitability. KD can be adapted to resource-constrained deployment, domain adaptation, privacy- or data-limited settings, and to improve adversarial robustness when paired with targeted techniques. Combining KD with complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning, structured sparsity, layer mapping) yields practical, high-quality compressed models across modalities including vision, language, graphs, and generative models.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Contemporary Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. Across computer vision and natural language processing, a wide family of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, multi-teacher and online schemes, many-to-many layer mappings, and task-aware layer selection—has been developed to trade off accuracy, latency, and model size for practical deployment. Empirical work shows that combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware transformations) and adapting distillation signals to task and data constraints yields compact models that capture much of teacher performance. At the same time, distillation must contend with capacity mismatch, robustness and distribution-shift sensitivity, privacy concerns, and the need for principled layer- and signal-alignment strategies—areas that motivate continued methodological and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural networks so they can run efficiently in production and on resource-constrained devices. Recent work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and that a range of complementary techniques—data augmentation, multi-teacher schedules, internal representation matching, layer alignment, meta-learning of teachers, and robustness-aware objectives—meaningfully improve student quality or transfer desirable properties. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on optimization, the choice of teacher/student architectures, and the distributional complexity of the training data. I argue that best practice for KD in deep learning and NLP is to treat it as a family of methods to be combined—augmenting data, distilling intermediate representations, leveraging multiple or adaptive teachers, and explicitly distilling robustness—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are mature, diverse strategies to reduce the computational and memory costs of large deep models while retaining much of their task performance. Approaches span architecture-level methods that search or prune for compact student networks, training-time methods that transfer dark knowledge via logits or intermediate representations, and data-centric methods that operate when original training data are unavailable. Empirical work shows success compressing large language models into lightweight networks for NLP tasks, highlights task- and data-specific pitfalls (notably for low-frequency tokens in sequence tasks), and motivates specialized extensions in federated and domain-adaptive settings. Theory and interpretive analyses have begun to clarify why distillation helps generalization and optimization, and recent work advocates shaping teachers to be more student-friendly or designing student-aware compression procedures. Overall, the literature shows a practical toolkit of complementary techniques—task-adaptive architecture search, feature- and attention-based matching, adversarial or synthetic-data distillation, and teacher-student co-training—each with trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to teacher behavior.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: Practical Knowledge Distillation for Deploying Large NLP and Deep Models: A Unified Argument for Multi-Teacher, Data-Agnostic, and Federated Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and essential set of techniques for compressing large deep and language models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. A mature KD strategy must simultaneously preserve teacher knowledge, generalize across domains and distributions, and respect deployment constraints (e.g., lack of original data or heterogeneous client devices). Empirical and methodological advances show that combining multi-teacher strategies, data-agnostic/distillation-from-generator approaches, feature-level projectors or ensembles, targeted augmentation, and adaptations for federated settings yields robust, efficient student models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates many strategies for transferring information from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. The field encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft logits), imitating intermediate representations, transferring structural or relational knowledge, and combining distillation with architecture changes, data augmentation, or privacy- and communication-aware protocols. Across computer vision, generation, recommendation, and many NLP tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in parameters and latency while often preserving most of the original performance; success depends on which knowledge is transferred, how architectures are aligned, data availability, and capacity/robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression across Modalities
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic for transferring soft logits to a rich family of techniques that enable deployment of large models in resource-constrained settings. Across NLP, vision, generative modeling, and cross-modal systems, distillation methods that match intermediate representations, adapt teacher signals to student inputs, exploit many-to-many layer correspondences, and combine with pruning or ensemble guidance consistently produce compact models with near-teacher performance. KD is also effective for domain adaptation and continual learning, making it a practical foundation for producing small, fast, and robust models for real-world applications.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring useful predictive behavior and representations from a teacher to a student. Methods span matching teacher output distributions (soft labels), aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, adversarial or data-free approaches, and online or federated variants that trade communication and privacy constraints against fidelity. Practical success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to manage imperfect or heterogeneous data and devices, and whether to combine distillation with complementary compression strategies (e.g., pruning or architecture search). While distilled students often retain much of a teacher's performance and enable deployment under latency or resource constraints, open challenges include preserving rare-token behaviors, handling domain shift and robustness, and designing privacy- and communication-efficient protocols for real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or multi-modal deep models into smaller, more deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or other structured knowledge. Work across vision, speech, and NLP shows a range of mechanisms (soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, layer mapping, and feature/attention guidance) and adaptations for limited or private data. Empirical results indicate distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while greatly reducing size and inference cost, but effectiveness depends on what knowledge is distilled, how it is represented, and the training regime.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques enable transfer of predictive power from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The literature has expanded beyond soft-label matching to include internal-representation distillation, module replacement, self-distillation, selective sample transfer, and adaptations for constraints such as privacy, communication, and low-precision inference. Applied across domains—from NLP rankers and translation to graph, vision-language, and speech systems—these methods trade off fidelity, efficiency, and robustness through a variety of algorithmic and engineering solutions.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Work across NLP and broader deep learning has developed multiple KD paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate-representation matching, layer-to-layer and many-to-many layer mapping, multi-teacher aggregation, and data-free distillation—and combined KD with other compression methods such as quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical results show that well-designed distillation can yield compact models that approach the accuracy of large pre-trained models while offering substantial savings in parameters, latency, and computational cost. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, coping with limited or unavailable training data, and selecting or weighting multiple teachers per example. The literature suggests principled strategies—attention-based layer fusion, representation-level losses, teacher confidence or dynamic weighting, and synthetic-data generation—that mitigate these issues and enable effective deployment of compressed models in domain-specific and resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad set of teacher→student techniques used to compress models, transfer inductive biases, and adapt models across domains while retaining performance. Work across vision, generative models, graph and language tasks shows KD can target soft logits, intermediate representations, and structural or relational knowledge; it can be applied with single or multiple teachers, combined with architectural changes, or used as a signal for automated search. Recent advances expand KD beyond mere logit-matching to feature-mimicking, progressive module replacement, and confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, while theory and empirical studies clarify when soft labels help, when hard labels correct imperfect teachers, and how distillation interacts with regularization. KD has also been used to mitigate fairness issues and to guide efficient architecture discovery. Together, these findings sketch a mature, diverse toolkit for compressing and adapting deep models across domains and modalities.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compression and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, multifaceted technique for compressing large models while often preserving — and sometimes improving — task performance. KD can transfer ensemble behaviour, provide regularization benefits, enable deployment under privacy or communication constraints, and be adapted to domain-specific and generation tasks. Practical KD implementations leverage ensembles, feature-level projectors, data augmentation, self-distillation, or data-free/federated protocols depending on resource and data availability. This paper argues that KD should be treated not only as a compression trick but as a general-purpose training paradigm with distinct theoretical and practical consequences for representation quality, robustness, and deployability.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, multi-faceted approach for compressing large neural networks into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Beyond simple teacher-student logits matching, distillation can be adapted to transfer inductive biases, deploy in federated or privacy-constrained settings, operate without access to original training data, and improve robustness and domain specialization. When combined with techniques such as feature mimicking, careful soft-label regularization, and online or ensemble-based training regimes, distillation provides a flexible toolkit to meet the efficiency, privacy, and deployment constraints of modern deep learning and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable paradigm for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller, more efficient students. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, KD methods—ranging from matching teacher output distributions to aligning intermediate representations and relational structure—enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to obtain or synthesize training data, and whether to complement distillation with adversarial or ensemble signals. When these elements are chosen and tuned for task and deployment constraints, KD produces compact models that are effective in resource-limited and application-specific settings.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Practical Directions for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compress large models into lightweight students for deployment. Recent work shows that KD can preserve most of a teacher's performance while dramatically reducing model size or computational cost, but gains depend on what knowledge is transferred, how teachers and students are prepared, and the distillation protocol. I argue that (1) transferring richer information than final logits, (2) preparing students with pre-training, (3) augmenting or synthesizing data during distillation, and (4) co-optimizing architecture-aware compression with distillation together form a robust recipe for reliable compression in NLP and other domains. These directions address generalization, data scarcity, and architectural differences, and they are supported by recent empirical and methodological studies across speech, vision, retrieval, and language modeling.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Remaining Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, flexible strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in parameters and latency, and it generalizes across settings from data-poor or privacy-sensitive deployments to multi-teacher and online training regimes. However, practical success depends on careful choice of what to transfer (logits, features, relations), handling limited or absent training data, mitigating transferred biases, and aligning teacher-student architectures. I argue that KD should be the primary tool in production compression pipelines but must be combined with data synthesis, teacher selection/calibration, and fairness-aware design to realize robust, reliable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking large deep models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable models while retaining much of their performance. Research has expanded beyond the original logit-based teacher-student paradigm to include feature mimicking, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, multi-teacher and adaptive-teacher strategies, and task- or hardware-aware compression. These methods have been applied across modalities — including vision, graphs, generative models, and a broad set of NLP tasks — and are increasingly combined with architecture search and pruning to meet deployment constraints. Despite empirical successes, important questions remain about what knowledge is most useful to transfer, how to select or adapt teachers, and how to operate under data, compute, or privacy limitations.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural networks so they can run efficiently in production and on resource-constrained devices. Recent work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and that a range of complementary techniques—data augmentation, multi-teacher schedules, internal representation matching, layer alignment, meta-learning of teachers, and robustness-aware objectives—meaningfully improve student quality or transfer desirable properties. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on optimization, the choice of teacher/student architectures, and the distributional complexity of the training data. I argue that best practice for KD in deep learning and NLP is to treat it as a family of methods to be combined—augmenting data, distilling intermediate representations, leveraging multiple or adaptive teachers, and explicitly distilling robustness—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, higher-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). In practice KD has been applied to compress large pre-trained language models, enable fast inference in NLP, adapt models to new domains or tasks, support heterogeneous and federated settings, and enable data-free scenarios. Approaches differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single vs multi-teacher, jointly trained teachers), and how training data is used or synthesized. Empirical results show KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of task performance, but success depends on choices around layer mapping, feature vs. logit supervision, data complexity, and training protocols. Open challenges include handling data heterogeneity, optimizing teacher-student pairings, and ensuring stable distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Walters
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central—but Not Sufficient—Tool for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a heuristic for shrinking ensembles into a broad, adaptable paradigm for producing deployable deep and NLP models. KD methods transfer information via softened outputs, intermediate representation matching, layer-wise alignment, and online or self-distillation, and they are most effective when combined with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to handle limited or private data. However, KD alone faces practical limits—data and domain mismatch, capacity gaps between teacher and student, and the need to preserve rare or safety-critical behaviors—so practitioners should treat KD as a central component of a compression toolkit rather than a universal solution.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical path to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A range of KD mechanisms—including soft-target supervision, intermediate feature or attention matching, multi-teacher fusion, data-free synthesis, and input-side augmentation—enable tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, privacy, and robustness. KD works best when its components are selected and adapted to deployment constraints: student capacity, available (or private) data, domain shift, and adversarial threats. However, important limitations remain, including distributional mismatch between teacher and student inputs, the preservation of robustness and fairness properties, and principled teacher selection. This article argues that a hybrid, constraint-aware KD strategy that combines representation-level transfer, data augmentation, and robustness- or privacy-aware synthesis offers the most reliable route to practical compression in real-world NLP and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or other learned structure. Methods span data-dependent distillation using teacher soft targets and intermediate hints, multi-teacher and ensemble compression, many-to-many layer mapping for large pre-trained language models, data-free or zero-shot distillation where training data are unavailable, and approaches that combine distillation with quantization or pruning for deployment. Empirical results demonstrate that distillation can recover much of a teacher's accuracy while enabling efficiency gains, but trade-offs remain around robustness, optimization difficulty, domain shifts, and the need for careful alignment of inputs or representations. Recent work addresses these challenges with generative replay, adversarial objectives, layer-matching distances, and teacher-annealing strategies, yet open problems include theory of optimization, scalable privacy-preserving protocols, and balancing fairness or robustness with compression.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques reduce model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger or more informed models to smaller ones. Methods vary from soft-label supervision and layer mapping to data-free generation, adversarial sample selection, federated and privacy-preserving protocols, and task- or domain-aware adaptation. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, and generative modeling show that distillation can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, but performance depends sensitively on what information is transferred, how samples are selected, and whether pretraining or task adaptation is used. Practical use favors hybrids that combine architectural search, selective or weighted distillation, and generation or rehearsal strategies when original data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile tool for transferring functionality from large, expensive models to smaller, more efficient ones across modalities. When properly applied, KD can enable deployment of compact models with competitive accuracy, but its effectiveness depends on dataset complexity, selection of distilled signals, and complementary compression strategies. This paper synthesizes empirical findings and method-level advances to argue for principled, task-aware KD workflows that mitigate common pitfalls while maximizing compression gains.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. Methods include soft-target or logit matching, feature- and layer-level mimicry, multi-teacher and ensemble-driven transfer, data-free or zero-shot approaches, and combinations with pruning or quantization. Distillation works both as a mechanism for transmitting ‘‘dark knowledge’’ about class relationships and as a regularizer that can improve student generalization, but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, data or synthetic inputs, teacher design, and alignment between teacher and student. Practical goals—reducing inference cost, enabling edge deployment, preserving accuracy under domain shift, and meeting privacy or fairness constraints—are achievable in many settings but require task- and data-aware design. Open problems include robust, privacy-preserving distillation without teacher data, principled teacher selection and weighting, theoretical understanding of optimization gaps, and balancing compression with fairness and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Flexible Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit: it can transfer logits, internal representations, or structured relational knowledge; it can be combined with architecture search, multi-teacher schemes, or data synthesis; and it can be adapted with task-aware filtering or teacher-aware training to address capacity mismatch and deployment constraints. Carefully chosen distillation targets, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression components produce small, deployable models that retain much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, or privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, and Evolving Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core engineering and research paradigm for compressing large models into efficient students while preserving accuracy and desirable behaviors. KD encompasses soft-target transfer, intermediate representation alignment, ensemble-to-single compression, and complementary data- and architecture-aware techniques. When treated as a design problem—choosing which signals to transfer, how to align representations, and how to manage data constraints—KD enables deployment across resource-limited and domain-shifted settings, but open challenges remain in preserving rare-token behaviors, coping with imperfect teachers, and operating without original data.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from large teacher models to smaller students to enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Methods extend beyond matching teacher logits to include feature- and attention-level transfer, multi-teacher and staged pipelines, data- and augmentation-aware protocols, and combinations with low-precision or architecture-aware compression. Empirical results across vision, language, graph, and generation tasks show that careful selection of what to transfer, how to prepare students, and how to handle data mismatches determines the practical trade-offs between model size, speed, and retained performance. Open problems include robustness under data scarcity, heterogeneous architecture alignment, and preserving rare-token or domain-specific behaviors during compression.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural knowledge. Methods span matching softened output distributions, feature- and attention-level imitation, layer mapping and progressive module replacement, channel- and module-aware transfers, and data-free or generative approaches for when original training data are unavailable. Practical pipelines combine KD with quantization, low-precision training, pruning, or architecture transformations and often rely on staged or adaptive teacher-student schedules. Empirical evidence shows KD can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across vision and NLP tasks, but success depends on teacher quality, what and which samples are distilled, data availability, and careful engineering of interfaces between heterogeneous teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a diverse toolkit for transferring information from larger, more expensive models to smaller, faster, or more constrained models. Methods range from matching output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, altering training curricula, and designing compression-aware teachers or architectures. These approaches have been applied across domains including vision, speech, translation, retrieval, and on-device deployment, and have been adapted to privacy- and communication-constrained settings. Empirical and analytical work has clarified different mechanisms by which distillation aids learning, and recent work explores automation, adversarial feature transfer, sample selection, and architecture-aware strategies to improve efficiency without sacrificing much performance.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are widely used to transfer behavior from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling deployment under resource constraints. Research over the past decade has developed variants that target outputs (soft labels), internal representations (layer-wise and attention-based methods), data regimes (data-free or distilled training sets), and architecture search for task-aware compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the practical gains and fundamental limits of distillation, and points to best practices such as pre-training compact models, selecting or synthesizing appropriate training data, and aligning student capacity to distilled signal.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Practical Strengths and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach to compress large or expensive models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their predictive power. Across vision, speech, ranking, and natural language processing, KD enables deployment of lightweight architectures by transferring dark knowledge, feature-level signals, or ensemble behavior from teacher models. However, distillation success depends on a set of interacting choices—teacher preparation, student architecture, which signals are transferred, data and augmentation strategies, and optimization—so KD is a powerful tool when combined with careful design but not an automatic solution for all compression needs. This paper synthesizes empirical lessons and provides actionable recommendations for applying KD effectively in practice.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are central tools for converting large, high-performing deep models into smaller, faster models that are practical for deployment. A broad repertoire of methods exists—matching soft logits, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial and online co-training, and data- or task-aware augmentation—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical evidence shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, but success depends on how teacher signals are represented, what data are used, and how architecture or domain mismatches are addressed. Practical deployment requires attention to data availability, privacy or federated constraints, teacher errors, and optimization stability; promising directions include pre-training compact students, online and federated distillation protocols, and specialized layer- or modality-aware objectives.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Capabilities, Mechanisms, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When applied thoughtfully—choosing appropriate distillation targets, preparing the student (often via pre-training), and addressing data, privacy, and robustness constraints—KD yields compact models that retain a substantial fraction of teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks. However, its success depends on design choices (what to distill and when), data availability, and mitigation of teacher errors; thus KD is best treated as a system of complementary techniques rather than a single recipe.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core and a Bounded Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and flexible approach for compressing large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with task-aware objectives, intermediate representation alignment, appropriate data strategies (including synthetic-data approaches), and architecture-aware design, KD yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance and enable deployment in resource-constrained or heterogeneous environments. However, KD has predictable failure modes—capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity, propagation of teacher errors, and optimization fragility—that demand complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful protocol design to realize reliable compression in practice.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Responses
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural signals. Across vision and NLP, KD variants—logit/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, multi- and self-teaching, and combinations with pruning/quantization—enable reduced inference cost and on-device deployment while attempting to retain performance. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD acts both as a route to transfer representational inductive biases and as a form of learned regularization; its success depends on signal choice, data provenance, capacity mismatch, and optimization. Methodological refinements (data augmentation, adversarial or boundary-focused examples, data-free synthesis, teacher design, and divergence choices) address core challenges in practice, but open problems remain around robustness, privacy, fairness, and reliably closing the teacher–student performance gap.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across tasks and modalities. KD's benefits arise from multiple mechanisms: transferring soft output distributions, mimicking intermediate features, providing regularization that improves generalization, and enabling compression even when original training data are unavailable. Empirically and theoretically, KD should be treated as a toolbox: select loss forms (logit, feature, relational), augment or synthesize data when needed, and consider joint training of teacher and student or teacher design that is friendly to students. Combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, pruning, architecture design), KD helps produce efficient models that retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting real deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Practical, Private, and Robust Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is often framed narrowly as a model-compression trick to shrink large neural networks. This paper argues KD should instead be viewed as a core engineering and scientific tool for practical deployment: it enables training with limited or private data, yields task- and domain-adaptive compact models, improves robustness and fairness, and transfers intermediate representations and attention patterns that standard supervised training cannot. We synthesize evidence from recent work to show how variants of KD—self-distillation, layer-wise projection, multi-teacher schemes, teacher annealing, and data-free distillation—address concrete deployment challenges in vision and NLP, and we derive practical recommendations for combining these techniques in real systems.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Engine for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a heuristic into a set of principled, modality-agnostic techniques that enable deployment of high-capacity models in resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings. By transferring predictive behaviour and internal representations from large teachers to compact students, distillation preserves much of the teacher's utility while enabling large speed, memory, and communication gains. Recent advances show that combining representation-level matching, teacher–student co-design, data-free synthesis, and task-adaptive compression yields robust, practical pipelines for compressing models across vision, language, graph, and federated settings.
