papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. It has evolved from straightforward soft-label training to richer objectives that match features, attention, or module behaviors, and to deployment-aware variants that address privacy, data scarcity, and heterogeneous devices. Empirical work across vision and language shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation signals, data, and architecture choices are carefully matched; important open problems include data heterogeneity, capacity mismatch, bias transfer, and theoretical understanding of what is actually transferred.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and/or internal representations. A rich set of mechanisms—soft-target (logit) matching, feature or representation imitation, layer-wise mapping, multi-teacher and ensemble-to-student transfers, and data-free or privacy-aware strategies—has been developed and combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical evidence shows distilled students can recover much of teacher accuracy while substantially reducing latency and footprint, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, data and augmentation strategies, teacher quality, and training schedules. Ongoing work focuses on robustness to domain shift, heterogeneous devices, limited or unavailable data, and principled ways to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural networks so they can run efficiently in production and on resource-constrained devices. Recent work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and that a range of complementary techniques—data augmentation, multi-teacher schedules, internal representation matching, layer alignment, meta-learning of teachers, and robustness-aware objectives—meaningfully improve student quality or transfer desirable properties. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on optimization, the choice of teacher/student architectures, and the distributional complexity of the training data. I argue that best practice for KD in deep learning and NLP is to treat it as a family of methods to be combined—augmenting data, distilling intermediate representations, leveraging multiple or adaptive teachers, and explicitly distilling robustness—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of practical and theoretical approaches for shrinking deep models while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, layer- and feature-level matching, architecture-aware transformations, teacher improvement or selection strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving pipelines, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-transfer applications, recent work shows that careful design choices—such as how layers are matched, which features to transfer, whether the teacher is static or trained to teach, and how to handle limited or private data—substantially affect the student’s final accuracy and deployment efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their performance. KD operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, relational structure) and can be combined with complementary compression techniques and data strategies to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When tailored to model architecture, task demands, and available data, KD yields compact models that enable real-world deployment across modalities and domains.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass a set of techniques that transfer knowledge from larger, expensive models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students) so the students retain much of the teacher utility while fitting deployment constraints. Research has produced a variety of distillation paradigms: logit- and soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, layer-wise and channel-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, self-supervised distillation, multi-teacher ensembles and domain-aware adaptation. Empirical work shows that combining pre-training for compact architectures with distillation, using task-aware selection of teacher signals, and tailoring distillation to modality- or task-specific structure leads to stronger compressed models. Important open issues include distillation without access to original data, preserving fairness and privacy in compressed models, and closing the capacity gap between teacher and student without over-constraining the student.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compression and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, multifaceted technique for compressing large models while often preserving — and sometimes improving — task performance. KD can transfer ensemble behaviour, provide regularization benefits, enable deployment under privacy or communication constraints, and be adapted to domain-specific and generation tasks. Practical KD implementations leverage ensembles, feature-level projectors, data augmentation, self-distillation, or data-free/federated protocols depending on resource and data availability. This paper argues that KD should be treated not only as a compression trick but as a general-purpose training paradigm with distinct theoretical and practical consequences for representation quality, robustness, and deployability.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Challenges, and Practical Advances
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior or intermediate representations. Research has developed many variants — logits-based soft-labels, feature- and attention-based matching, layer-wise and task-aware filters, self-distillation, and data-free approaches — and applied them across vision, language, recommendation, and healthcare. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the practical benefits (faster inference, lower memory, domain adaptation, interpretability) and core limitations (optimization obstacles, capacity mismatch, distributional effects), motivating techniques that alter what is distilled, how it is matched, and even how teachers are trained to be more amenable to students.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks, a consistent set of practices has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, intermediate-layer matching, and task- or domain-specific adaptation—augmented by variants that address missing data, distributed training, privacy, and teacher-student mismatch. Empirical results show that distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while enjoying large gains in inference speed and memory, and recent work clarifies when and why distillation acts as an effective regularizer.

papers_seen.author: Figueroa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies condense large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or lower-precision students suitable for deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Research has produced a taxonomy of approaches—soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate/feature imitation, relational or attention-based losses, multi-teacher fusion, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates that properly designed distillation pipelines can preserve most teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling substantial gains in inference speed and memory; theoretical analyses attribute much of KD’s benefit to regularization from soft targets and the transfer of inductive biases. Remaining challenges include handling teacher–student capacity mismatch, preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors, operating without original training data, and designing adaptive, task-aware distillation signals.

papers_seen.author: Dixon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods compress large deep models into smaller, faster, or more private models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature shows a spectrum of KD signals (soft logits, intermediate features, layer mappings), enhancements via data interventions and architecture search, and combinations with pruning or low-precision inference. Practical success depends on task- and deployment-aware choices (which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, what augmentations or synthetic data to use) as well as attention to privacy and robustness. The field has produced effective recipes for compressing pretrained language models, vision transformers, and generative models, while ongoing work clarifies limits and complementary techniques for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression across Modalities and Deployment Constraints
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from a teacher to a student, KD can preserve accuracy while reducing model size and inference cost. Combining KD with task-aware objectives, data-augmentation strategies, and data-free synthesis techniques further extends its applicability to settings with limited task data, privacy constraints, or strict latency requirements. This paper argues that a principled, hybrid KD approach—tailored to the modality and deployment constraints—offers the best path to deployable, high-quality compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide a broad, practically oriented toolkit for shrinking large neural models while retaining most of their performance. Methods include transferring soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, adapting teacher or student architectures, using adversarial or data-free sample generation, and combining distillation with quantization or pruning. Empirical results across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks show substantial latency and memory gains; success depends on what signals are transferred, how layers are matched, data availability and augmentation, and the deployment constraints that shape algorithmic choices.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Responses
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural signals. Across vision and NLP, KD variants—logit/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, multi- and self-teaching, and combinations with pruning/quantization—enable reduced inference cost and on-device deployment while attempting to retain performance. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD acts both as a route to transfer representational inductive biases and as a form of learned regularization; its success depends on signal choice, data provenance, capacity mismatch, and optimization. Methodological refinements (data augmentation, adversarial or boundary-focused examples, data-free synthesis, teacher design, and divergence choices) address core challenges in practice, but open problems remain around robustness, privacy, fairness, and reliably closing the teacher–student performance gap.

papers_seen.author: Ortiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, mature toolkit for turning large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Approaches vary from transferring softened outputs to aligning intermediate representations or relational structure, from online and multi-teacher schemes to data-free and privacy-aware pipelines. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and other modalities shows that well-designed distillation can preserve most of a teacher's performance while delivering substantial reductions in inference cost, parameter count, and memory footprint. Practical success depends on matching distillation targets and schedules to student capacity and deployment constraints, handling limited or private data appropriately, and addressing robustness, fairness, and distribution-shift concerns.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Design-Sensitive Path to Compact Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation offers a practical route to compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students that retain much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness arises from multiple distillation signals (soft labels, intermediate representations, attention or channel maps) and from combining distillation with pre-training, architecture-aware design, and data-management strategies. However, realizing these gains in real systems requires explicit choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited, private or heterogeneous data.

papers_seen.author: Pham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical set of techniques to transfer predictive and representational knowledge from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across computer vision, generative modeling, retrieval, and natural language processing, practitioners use KD to reduce inference cost, enable on-device deployment, and adapt models to new domains or privacy constraints. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps), how teacher and student are aligned (layer mapping, attention-weighted projection, task-aware filters), and whether original training data are available (data-free and zero-shot approaches). Success depends on careful choices of teacher preparation, student capacity and architecture, signal selection, and data or synthetic-sample strategies; when designed appropriately, KD combined with complementary compression (pruning, architecture transforms) yields compact models with strong empirical performance, while important limitations remain (representation mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, low-frequency token coverage).

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical but Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones. When used thoughtfully, KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on which signals are transferred (logits, features, relational information), alignment between teacher and student, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and awareness of teacher imperfections. Combining KD with representation-level matching, task-aware layer alignment, online or federated protocols, and data strategies yields the best trade-offs for real systems.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques condense information from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable ones. Across vision, speech, recommendation, generative models, and natural language processing, practitioners use a mix of logit-based soft-label supervision, feature imitation, data distillation, multi-teacher fusion, curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware search to trade accuracy for latency, memory, or interpretability. Empirical work shows distilled students can often approach teacher accuracy while enabling deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings; theoretical and empirical analyses attribute much of KD’s effectiveness to the regularizing properties of soft targets, while recent extensions explicitly address adversarial robustness, decision-boundary transfer, domain adaptation, continual learning, and task-specific constraints. Remaining challenges include preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors (e.g., low-frequency phenomena), designing teacher-free or data-free alternatives, and building principled curricula and multi-source transfers that maximize student utility in downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable tool for reducing model size and inference cost while preserving (or even improving) performance. Beyond straightforward teacher→student logit matching, KD can be applied structurally (transforming architectures without redesign), combined with quantization, used for domain adaptation of large pretrained language models, leveraged in multi-teacher and few-shot settings, and operated without access to original data. KD’s benefits arise both from transferring predictive behavior and from inducing effective regularization; when paired with careful choices (e.g., feature projectors, divergence measures, or pseudo-replay for data-free settings), KD enables deployment of compact, reliable models across vision, speech, language, graph, and generative-model domains.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical and Multifaceted Engine for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical set of techniques that enable deploying high-performing deep models under computation, memory, data, and privacy constraints. By transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure from large teachers to compact students, KD supports domain specialization, model acceleration, privacy-preserving release, and improved generalization. Best results come from matching the KD strategy to the constraints and goals of the application (e.g., multi-teacher aggregation, representation-level transfer, data-free generation, or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relations. Across vision and natural language tasks, KD variants—logits/soft-label matching, feature- and relation-level imitation, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—enable substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often retaining most of the teacher’s performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to generate or curate data for transfer, and how to align teacher and student capacity; common extensions address fairness, federated or distributed settings, and privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors (especially on low-frequency phenomena), domain and device heterogeneity, and preserving robustness under distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable paradigm for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller, more efficient students. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, KD methods—ranging from matching teacher output distributions to aligning intermediate representations and relational structure—enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to obtain or synthesize training data, and whether to complement distillation with adversarial or ensemble signals. When these elements are chosen and tuned for task and deployment constraints, KD produces compact models that are effective in resource-limited and application-specific settings.

papers_seen.author: Lambert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring aspects of teacher behavior. The field has expanded from soft-label (logit) supervision to diverse strategies including feature- and representation-level imitation, flexible layer mapping, online/co-distillation, data- and domain-aware augmentation, and multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends on what is transferred (soft targets, features, relations), how teacher and student architectures are aligned, the availability and quality of distillation data, and deployment constraints such as privacy, domain shift, and compute budget. Open challenges include selecting the right distillation targets for task and capacity gap, ensuring robustness and fairness post-compression, and automating adaptive distillation pipelines for heterogeneous production settings.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are widely used to transfer predictive behavior and representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. A broad family of methods—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and layer-level mimicry, multi-teacher fusion, online and teacher-free protocols, and data-free or privacy-aware synthesis—has been developed and evaluated across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Empirical studies show that, when designed carefully (teacher selection, data strategy, and objective choice), KD can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling practical deployment; however, limitations remain around domain shift, robustness, preservation of fine-grained behaviors, and data- or architecture-mismatch, motivating hybrid strategies that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware training.

papers_seen.author: Frost
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable means to compress large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. When matched to task constraints—choosing what teacher signals to transfer, how to align layers or features, and whether or how to handle missing or private training data—KD enables deployment of competitive models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: careful design (task-aware layer selection, many-to-many mapping for large pre-trained transformers, selective sample weighting, and data-free procedures when needed) is required to avoid propagating teacher errors, worsening robustness, or underfitting compact students. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central compression engine for modern deep learning and NLP pipelines, but that success depends on matching KD mechanisms to application constraints and combining KD with complementary engineering (efficient distillation pipelines and synthetic-data or adversarial generators when data are unavailable).

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for creating smaller, faster models from larger ones while retaining much of their functionality. When combined with representation matching, architecture-aware surgery, selective sample strategies, and privacy-aware protocols, KD enables deployment of high-quality models across modalities and constrained environments. However, its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; without such care, distillation can underperform or transfer undesirable behaviors. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central, composable tool in compression toolkits, and outlines concrete methodological priorities that practitioners should follow to realize reliable, efficient distilled models.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from large, often expensive teacher models into smaller or more efficient student models. Research has developed diverse KD mechanisms — soft-label distillation, intermediate feature matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data-centric augmentations — and applied them across domains (vision, multimodal, language, graph, and generative models). Empirical work demonstrates KD can retain much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and theoretical and empirical analyses link KD to regularization effects (e.g., label smoothing and bias–variance tradeoffs). Practical adaptations address modality misalignment, low-resource data, robustness to adversaries, and task-specific compression. Remaining challenges include principled teacher selection, distributional mismatch between distilled and original data, and scaling KD to large multimodal and structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central paradigm for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Research spans theoretical analyses of when and why distillation helps, practical methods for compressing pretrained language models, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, strategies to preserve robustness, and distributed/federated adaptations. Methods include soft-label matching, intermediate feature/attention imitation, many-to-many layer mappings, task-adaptive architecture search, and self-distillation. Empirical and theoretical work highlights gains in efficiency and deployment feasibility across vision and NLP tasks, while also revealing limitations related to data distribution, teacher quality, robustness, and low-frequency token coverage. Open directions include principled handling of imperfect teachers, domain adaptation during compression, robustness-aware distillation, and scalable distillation in distributed or data-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Ross

Practical success depends on choices about teacher-student design, data availability and quality, and optimization strategies; contemporary work emphasizes combining representation-level objectives, teacher-friendly or teacher-free approaches, and data-aware training to produce robust, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques compress large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or lower-precision models while retaining much of their performance. Approaches range from matching teacher soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations and using contrastive or projection-based objectives. Practical training choices—such as which layers or features to mimic, how to filter or weight training samples, the role of data augmentation, and whether compact models are pre-trained—strongly affect outcomes. KD has been applied across domains (vision, language, graphs), combined with quantization and low-precision deployment, and adapted for resource-heterogeneous and latency-sensitive settings. Empirical and theoretical work highlights that KD works both by transferring relational/representational knowledge and by providing regularizing soft targets; effective distillation designs balance these mechanisms and tailor the transfer to task and capacity constraints.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) consolidates many strategies for transferring information from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. The field encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft logits), imitating intermediate representations, transferring structural or relational knowledge, and combining distillation with architecture changes, data augmentation, or privacy- and communication-aware protocols. Across computer vision, generation, recommendation, and many NLP tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in parameters and latency while often preserving most of the original performance; success depends on which knowledge is transferred, how architectures are aligned, data availability, and capacity/robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Compressing Visual-linguistic Model via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite exciting progress in pre-training for visual-linguistic (VL) representations, very few aspire to a small VL model. In this paper, we study knowledge distillation (KD) to effectively compress a transformer-based large VL model into a small VL model. The major challenge arises from the inconsistent regional visual tokens extracted from different detectors of Teacher and Student, resulting in the misalignment of hidden representations and attention distributions. To address the problem, we retrain and adapt the Teacher by using the same region proposals from Student's detector while the features are from Teacher's own object detector. With aligned network inputs, the adapted Teacher is capable of transferring the knowledge through the intermediate representations. Specifically, we use the mean square error loss to mimic the attention distribution inside the transformer block and present a token-wise noise contrastive loss to align the hidden state by contrasting with negative representations stored in a sample queue. To this end, we show that our proposed distillation significantly improves the performance of small VL models on image captioning and visual question answering tasks. It reaches 120.8 in CIDEr score on COCO captioning, an improvement of 5.1 over its non-distilled counterpart; and an accuracy of 69.8 on VQA 2.0, a 0.8 gain from the baseline. Our extensive experiments and ablations confirm the effectiveness of VL distillation in both pre-training and fine-tuning stages.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques compress large neural models into smaller, faster, or more private students by transferring information from a teacher. Research over the past decade has explored a spectrum of KD variants — from soft-label logits transfer to feature-map matching, adversarial and online schemes, few-shot and privacy-preserving compression, and theoretical analyses of when and why distillation helps. Empirical work shows KD improves deployment practicality across vision, speech, NLP, graph, and generative models, while recent studies examine robustness, data-efficiency, the role of pre-training, and the impact of teacher quality. Important open directions include principled methods for sample selection, cross-domain transfer, formal guarantees under limited data or adversaries, and integrating KD with compression primitives such as pruning and structured sparsity.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Rice
papers_seen.title: CoReD: Generalizing Fake Media Detection with Continual Representation using Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Over the last few decades, artificial intelligence research has made tremendous strides, but it still heavily relies on fixed datasets in stationary environments. Continual learning is a growing field of research that examines how AI systems can learn sequentially from a continuous stream of linked data in the same way that biological systems do. Simultaneously, fake media such as deepfakes and synthetic face images have emerged as significant to current multimedia technologies. Recently, numerous method has been proposed which can detect deepfakes with high accuracy. However, they suffer significantly due to their reliance on fixed datasets in limited evaluation settings. Therefore, in this work, we apply continuous learning to neural networks' learning dynamics, emphasizing its potential to increase data efficiency significantly. We propose Continual Representation using Distillation (CoReD) method that employs the concept of Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). We design CoReD to perform sequential domain adaptation tasks on new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets, while effectively minimizing the catastrophic forgetting in a teacher-student model setting. Our extensive experimental results demonstrate that our method is efficient at domain adaptation to detect low-quality deepfakes videos and GAN-generated images from several datasets, outperforming the-state-of-art baseline methods.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. When applied thoughtfully—selecting what to transfer (logits, features, attention), aligning inputs and architectures, and combining KD with complementary compression (pruning, structured sparsity, quantization) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic samples, curriculum)—KD enables resource-efficient deployment across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings. However, its success depends on teacher quality, data availability, and alignment between teacher and student; addressing these constraints through multi-teacher designs, black-box adaptation, and feature-level alignment remains essential for robust, private, and high-performance compression.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking large deep models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable models while retaining much of their performance. Research has expanded beyond the original logit-based teacher-student paradigm to include feature mimicking, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, multi-teacher and adaptive-teacher strategies, and task- or hardware-aware compression. These methods have been applied across modalities — including vision, graphs, generative models, and a broad set of NLP tasks — and are increasingly combined with architecture search and pruning to meet deployment constraints. Despite empirical successes, important questions remain about what knowledge is most useful to transfer, how to select or adapt teachers, and how to operate under data, compute, or privacy limitations.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a primary tool for compressing large deep models into compact, deployable students while preserving much of the teacher’s performance. KD has been applied across modalities and use-cases—distilling large language models into lightweight encoders, compressing ensembles into single predictors, enabling privacy- and device-aware deployments, and even operating without access to original training data. At the same time, theoretical gaps, data- and heterogeneity-driven failure modes, and teacher biases motivate hybrid strategies (multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, data-free generators, and combined compression techniques) to realize KD’s full potential in practical systems.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide practical ways to transfer performance from large, expensive models to smaller, faster ones. The literature spans soft-label distillation from ensembles, feature- and representation-based matching, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, task-adaptive compression for large pretrained language models, and methods to transfer non-standard properties such as adversarial robustness. Empirical results demonstrate that properly designed distillation procedures can retain much of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, that internal-representation matching often improves downstream generalization beyond logits-only approaches, and that KD variants can be adapted to constraints such as limited (or private) data, distributed training, and resource- or latency-aware deployment. Open challenges include understanding which aspects of teacher knowledge are most useful for which student architectures and tasks, designing distillation under strict privacy or data-availability constraints, and transferring robustness properties reliably.

papers_seen.author: Wise
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Task-Aware Remedies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, flexible suite of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while often retaining most task performance. Empirical work demonstrates KD’s effectiveness across modalities and tasks, but also reveals systematic limitations arising from teacher-student capacity mismatch, optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and the sample-wise effects of soft targets. To make distillation reliably useful in production and research, practitioners should pair KD with task-aware layer selection, representation-level supervision, careful sample weighting, and complementary compression methods such as pruning or quantization. This balanced approach preserves KD’s deployment advantages while mitigating its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Practical Pathways for Compressing Large NLP Models: Pre-train the Student, Distill Carefully, and Guard for Data & Robustness
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach to compress large deep learning models for NLP and related tasks. When the student model is itself pre-trained, distillation yields especially strong and consistent gains; complementary methods — including data augmentation during distillation, progressive module replacement, ensemble teachers or teacher adaptation, and data-free or privacy-aware distillation — address common deployment constraints such as limited task data, inference cost, data access, and adversarial robustness. Combining these techniques and choosing distillation targets and schedules with theoretical and empirical guidance yields compact models that retain much of the original performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster ones by transferring information from one or more teacher models to a student model. Methods range from matching output distributions (soft logits) to aligning internal representations, using ensembles or multiple teachers, conducting distillation without access to original data, and employing self-distillation or teacher-adaptation strategies. Empirical work across vision and language shows that careful choices about what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to manage data constraints determine the trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and allied compression techniques have become central tools for reducing the computational and storage cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Research has expanded beyond the original soft-label paradigm to include distillation of internal representations, layer- and channel-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, and teacher-student co-design. Applications span vision, NLP, graph models, generative networks, and large-scale distributed training. Recent work also explores distillation for robustness, low-precision deployment, few-shot compression, and federated or multi-device settings. Despite strong empirical gains, open challenges remain in transferring inductive biases, choosing what and when to distill, and preserving attributes such as fairness and adversarial robustness in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are central tools for converting large, high-performing deep models into smaller, faster models that are practical for deployment. A broad repertoire of methods exists—matching soft logits, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial and online co-training, and data- or task-aware augmentation—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical evidence shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, but success depends on how teacher signals are represented, what data are used, and how architecture or domain mismatches are addressed. Practical deployment requires attention to data availability, privacy or federated constraints, teacher errors, and optimization stability; promising directions include pre-training compact students, online and federated distillation protocols, and specialized layer- or modality-aware objectives.
