papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Beyond Compression: Roles, Limits, and Best Practices for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly framed as a route to compress large models into smaller deployable students, but its benefits and pitfalls extend well beyond mere parameter reduction. KD acts as a form of learned regularization, can be applied in self-distillation and teacher-free regimes, and enables transferring properties such as robustness, privacy-preserving signals, and task-specific intermediate knowledge. At the same time, KD faces optimization and representation-mismatch challenges and can propagate undesirable biases from teacher to student. This paper argues that practitioners should treat KD as a flexible toolbox: combine soft-label supervision with internal-representation matching, flexible layer-mapping, attention-guided feature alignment, and targeted interventions for fairness, privacy, and robustness to get consistent benefits in both vision and NLP applications.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core practical approach for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while retaining much of the original performance. Multiple distillation mechanisms—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations, adversarial/ensemble-based transfer, and data-free or selective-sample techniques—allow KD to address constraints such as limited data, heterogeneous deployment, low-precision hardware, and domain shift. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a transfer of representational structure and as a regularizer; its success depends on choices about what is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, how training data (real or synthetic) are used, and which complementary compression methods are applied. Remaining practical challenges include distributional mismatch, heterogeneity of architectures and devices, and principled teacher selection and optimization strategies.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Mcmillan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Adaptive Tool for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the original performance. KD's successes across vision, speech, and NLP show that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention), how to align teacher and student, and whether to rely on original data or generated/synthetic data determines outcomes. To be effective in real deployments, KD must be combined with complementary methods (data-free generation, federated protocols, targeted augmentation, and robustness-aware objectives) and applied adaptively to task and resource constraints. When used thoughtfully, KD enables substantial efficiency gains without wholesale architectural redesign; when used naively it can propagate teacher errors or exacerbate distributional and low-frequency lexical problems.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical and Multifaceted Engine for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical set of techniques that enable deploying high-performing deep models under computation, memory, data, and privacy constraints. By transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure from large teachers to compact students, KD supports domain specialization, model acceleration, privacy-preserving release, and improved generalization. Best results come from matching the KD strategy to the constraints and goals of the application (e.g., multi-teacher aggregation, representation-level transfer, data-free generation, or progressive replacement).

papers_seen.author: Rasmussen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Compressing Deep Models in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach that enables deploying high-performing deep models by transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller students. KD operates through multiple mechanisms—matching soft outputs, imitating intermediate representations, and shaping relational structure—and can be combined with pre-training, architecture search, low-precision numerics, and data synthesis to meet real deployment constraints. When chosen and applied carefully (appropriate targets, student pre-training, layer mappings, and consideration of data/privacy/ethical constraints), KD yields compact models that retain much of teacher accuracy while being suitable for latency-, memory-, or privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Flexible Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is most effective when treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit: it can transfer logits, internal representations, or structured relational knowledge; it can be combined with architecture search, multi-teacher schemes, or data synthesis; and it can be adapted with task-aware filtering or teacher-aware training to address capacity mismatch and deployment constraints. Carefully chosen distillation targets, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression components produce small, deployable models that retain much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, or privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques condense information from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable ones. Across vision, speech, recommendation, generative models, and natural language processing, practitioners use a mix of logit-based soft-label supervision, feature imitation, data distillation, multi-teacher fusion, curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware search to trade accuracy for latency, memory, or interpretability. Empirical work shows distilled students can often approach teacher accuracy while enabling deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings; theoretical and empirical analyses attribute much of KD’s effectiveness to the regularizing properties of soft targets, while recent extensions explicitly address adversarial robustness, decision-boundary transfer, domain adaptation, continual learning, and task-specific constraints. Remaining challenges include preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors (e.g., low-frequency phenomena), designing teacher-free or data-free alternatives, and building principled curricula and multi-source transfers that maximize student utility in downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques reduce the size and runtime of large neural models by transferring information from one or more high-capacity teacher models to a smaller student model. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, methods vary in what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, relations, or latent experts), how training data are used (original data, distilled predictions, or no data), and how multiple or imperfect teachers are combined. Practical adaptations include task-specific losses, sample selection or weighting, and architectural transformations; KD is also integrated with system-level strategies such as federated learning and pruning to meet device constraints. Empirical results show KD can preserve much of teacher performance while substantially reducing compute and memory, but success depends on choices of teacher strength, data availability, multi-teacher aggregation, and whether task structure (e.g., localization or ranking) is explicitly addressed.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques aim to transfer predictive behavior from large, expensive models to smaller, faster models so they can be deployed under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Over the past decade research has produced a taxonomy of distillation mechanisms (logit/soft-target matching, representation or feature imitation, multi-teacher and ensemble-to-student transfers), adaptations for low-data or data-free settings, and combinations of distillation with architecture search and pruning. Empirical work shows that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance at large computational savings, but also highlights practical failure modes: students often do not perfectly match teacher predictive distributions, optimization choices and training data matter strongly, and specialized methods are needed for task-specific or distributed scenarios. Recent advances emphasize multi-stage/multi-teacher schedules, augmentation-aware objectives, online distributed training, and loss formulations that better capture teacher uncertainty; combining these approaches with automated architecture search and structured pruning yields stronger, hardware-aware compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Limitations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and richer internal signals. Techniques extend beyond matching teacher logits to include feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, adversarially-generated or adversarially-robust signals, online and multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. These methods enable deployment of compact models across vision and NLP tasks (including compressing pretrained transformers), improve efficiency on-device, and can sometimes preserve or even enhance robustness and generalization. Success depends on choices of distillation target, student architecture and capacity, the nature and availability of distillation data, and handling of domain or agent heterogeneity; open issues include transferring robustness reliably, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and principled handling of heterogeneous or private data sources.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and/or internal representations. A rich set of mechanisms—soft-target (logit) matching, feature or representation imitation, layer-wise mapping, multi-teacher and ensemble-to-student transfers, and data-free or privacy-aware strategies—has been developed and combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical evidence shows distilled students can recover much of teacher accuracy while substantially reducing latency and footprint, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, data and augmentation strategies, teacher quality, and training schedules. Ongoing work focuses on robustness to domain shift, heterogeneous devices, limited or unavailable data, and principled ways to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a core technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient students suitable for deployment. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Success depends on choosing appropriate distillation strategies that account for model structure, task specificity, data availability, and training dynamics. When tailored—via structural transformations, progressive module replacement, task-aware layer alignment, or data-centric augmentations—distillation consistently produces compact models that approach teacher accuracy and enable real-world use cases that would otherwise be impractical.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and allied compression techniques have become central tools for reducing the computational and storage cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Research has expanded beyond the original soft-label paradigm to include distillation of internal representations, layer- and channel-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, and teacher-student co-design. Applications span vision, NLP, graph models, generative networks, and large-scale distributed training. Recent work also explores distillation for robustness, low-precision deployment, few-shot compression, and federated or multi-device settings. Despite strong empirical gains, open challenges remain in transferring inductive biases, choosing what and when to distill, and preserving attributes such as fairness and adversarial robustness in compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide a broad, practically oriented toolkit for shrinking large neural models while retaining most of their performance. Methods include transferring soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, adapting teacher or student architectures, using adversarial or data-free sample generation, and combining distillation with quantization or pruning. Empirical results across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks show substantial latency and memory gains; success depends on what signals are transferred, how layers are matched, data availability and augmentation, and the deployment constraints that shape algorithmic choices.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Nuanced Path to Model Compression in NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques to transfer knowledge from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. When combined with complementary strategies — such as pre-training compact architectures, data augmentation, selective sample transfer, and module-level compression — KD can yield compact models that retain much of the teacher's utility. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on what is transferred, the availability and nature of data, teacher–student design, and optimization choices. Responsible deployment requires understanding both the practical strengths (efficiency, adaptability, applicability to privacy settings) and the limitations (data dependence, optimization gaps, possible degradation on rare or shifted inputs) of distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Conditional Endorsement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are indispensable tools for deploying high-capacity deep models in resource- and latency-constrained settings. When combined with architecture-aware strategies, task adaptation, and data-aware protocols, KD recovers much of teacher performance while enabling substantial speed and size reductions. However, distillation is not a universal remedy: optimization difficulties, domain and low-frequency token mismatches, privacy or data-availability constraints, and fairness concerns require tailored remedies. Effective compression thus integrates KD with architecture search, progressive replacement, data-free methods, and fairness- and federated-aware training to achieve reliable, deployable students.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of practical and theoretical approaches for shrinking deep models while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, layer- and feature-level matching, architecture-aware transformations, teacher improvement or selection strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving pipelines, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-transfer applications, recent work shows that careful design choices—such as how layers are matched, which features to transfer, whether the teacher is static or trained to teach, and how to handle limited or private data—substantially affect the student’s final accuracy and deployment efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across tasks and modalities. KD's benefits arise from multiple mechanisms: transferring soft output distributions, mimicking intermediate features, providing regularization that improves generalization, and enabling compression even when original training data are unavailable. Empirically and theoretically, KD should be treated as a toolbox: select loss forms (logit, feature, relational), augment or synthesize data when needed, and consider joint training of teacher and student or teacher design that is friendly to students. Combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, pruning, architecture design), KD helps produce efficient models that retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting real deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a logits-matching trick into a broad set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from large neural teachers. Modern KD variants transfer soft predictions, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structure; they are combined with data-centric practices (augmentation, synthetic and zero-shot data) and complementary compression (pruning, architecture search) to meet real-world latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work demonstrates strong gains in NLP (notably transformer compression) as well as vision, graphs, and federated settings, while theoretical and empirical studies reveal optimization challenges, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional/heterogeneity limitations. Practical pipelines favor pretraining or progressive replacement, representation-level matching, task-adaptive data strategies, and awareness of privacy and robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Capabilities, Limitations, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and graph domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, speed up training at scale, and allow transfer of robustness or domain expertise when carefully designed. However, successful distillation depends on alignment of teacher and student inputs/representations, the choice of distilled signals (logits, features, attention, or contrastive embeddings), and careful handling of privacy, robustness, and domain shift. Best practice combines representation-level matching, adaptive teacher strategies, confidence-aware multi-teacher fusion, and privacy- or robustness-aware objectives to meet practical constraints while maximizing student performance.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Limited Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach that enables deploying large models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints by transferring knowledge from teacher to student models. KD extends beyond simple logit matching to include representation-level transfer, attention- and feature-guided objectives, multi-teacher schedules, and integration with architecture search and pretraining. While KD reliably improves efficiency and can preserve many teacher behaviors, its success depends on choices of distillation targets, teacher preparation, student architecture, and data strategies; it can also amplify teacher errors or struggle under data heterogeneity, requiring complementary techniques and careful engineering for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Contemporary Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. Across computer vision and natural language processing, a wide family of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, multi-teacher and online schemes, many-to-many layer mappings, and task-aware layer selection—has been developed to trade off accuracy, latency, and model size for practical deployment. Empirical work shows that combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware transformations) and adapting distillation signals to task and data constraints yields compact models that capture much of teacher performance. At the same time, distillation must contend with capacity mismatch, robustness and distribution-shift sensitivity, privacy concerns, and the need for principled layer- and signal-alignment strategies—areas that motivate continued methodological and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression across Modalities
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic for transferring soft logits to a rich family of techniques that enable deployment of large models in resource-constrained settings. Across NLP, vision, generative modeling, and cross-modal systems, distillation methods that match intermediate representations, adapt teacher signals to student inputs, exploit many-to-many layer correspondences, and combine with pruning or ensemble guidance consistently produce compact models with near-teacher performance. KD is also effective for domain adaptation and continual learning, making it a practical foundation for producing small, fast, and robust models for real-world applications.

papers_seen.author: Jacobs
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. It has evolved from straightforward soft-label training to richer objectives that match features, attention, or module behaviors, and to deployment-aware variants that address privacy, data scarcity, and heterogeneous devices. Empirical work across vision and language shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation signals, data, and architecture choices are carefully matched; important open problems include data heterogeneity, capacity mismatch, bias transfer, and theoretical understanding of what is actually transferred.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and empirically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and deployment constraints, KD enables moving from research-stage, high-capacity architectures to resource-efficient models suitable for latency- and privacy-constrained production. Realizing KD's full potential requires attention to teacher quality, data and domain mismatches, and scalability; appropriate choices—representation-level objectives, multi-teacher signals, online protocols, and privacy-aware distillation—address these challenges and make KD a core tool for applied deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a multifaceted toolkit for shrinking large neural models while retaining much of their accuracy. Approaches include matching teacher outputs (soft logits), aligning intermediate representations or attention patterns, transforming architectures to be resource-efficient, and designing teacher–student curricula or multi-teacher aggregations. KD is applied across supervised, self-supervised, few-shot, federated, and privacy-constrained scenarios and is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align layers and capacity, and how to handle limited or sensitive data; when designed carefully, KD enables deployment of compact models for diverse NLP and vision tasks while exposing open questions about robustness, fairness, and distributional generalization.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in NLP and Deep Learning: Necessity, Challenges, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models and transferring desirable properties (accuracy, robustness, or representations) into smaller, deployable students. In NLP and related deep-learning domains, distillation enables the efficient use of pretrained teachers, supports domain adaptation and continual learning, and can be adapted for supervised, self-supervised, and adversarial objectives. However, naive distillation can degrade specific behaviors (e.g., lexical choices or uncertainty calibration) unless the distillation pipeline addresses alignment of inputs and representations, intermediate-layer supervision, the sample-wise effects of soft labels, and robustness transfer. I argue that distillation should be treated as a design problem—choosing which knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student representations, and when to expose students to raw or adversarial signals—to yield compact models that preserve both accuracy and desirable inductive properties.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relations. Across vision and natural language tasks, KD variants—logits/soft-label matching, feature- and relation-level imitation, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—enable substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often retaining most of the teacher’s performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to generate or curate data for transfer, and how to align teacher and student capacity; common extensions address fairness, federated or distributed settings, and privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors (especially on low-frequency phenomena), domain and device heterogeneity, and preserving robustness under distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Practical Centrality and Conditional Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core engineering and research tool to compress large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across tasks and modalities show KD can substantially reduce parameter counts and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, and KD integrates naturally with complementary techniques (low-precision numerics, architecture search, pruning, federated or privacy-aware pipelines). At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey solution: optimization difficulties, imperfect teachers, data heterogeneity, privacy constraints, and robustness concerns require careful design choices and hybrid strategies. Effective deployment therefore depends on selecting which knowledge to transfer, adapting distillation signals to data and architecture mismatches, and combining KD with targeted algorithmic and system-level adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their predictive performance. KD has matured beyond simple output-matching into a family of methods that transfer intermediate representations, attention or channel-wise signals, and task-specific inductive biases; it can operate under data scarcity or privacy constraints and can be combined with architecture search or other compression primitives to produce deployment-ready models. Successful application requires matching the distillation recipe to the task, student capacity, and deployment constraints and managing teacher imperfections and data mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical family of methods for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, faster, or constrained students. Techniques span matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning intermediate representations, layer-wise mappings, and data-centric strategies (augmentation, synthesized data, or data-free protocols). Effective deployments combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation) and training choices (pretraining, curriculum schedules, ensemble-to-single transfers). Despite broad empirical success across vision, language, retrieval, and generative tasks, KD requires attention to capacity mismatch, data availability, and optimization dynamics to realize robust, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Flexible Core Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not a single recipe but a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large models into compact students suitable for deployment. When combined with task-aware architecture choices, ensemble or self-generated signals, and orthogonal compression methods, KD reliably reduces inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. Careful attention to what is distilled, data strategy, and training dynamics mitigates common failure modes and enables robust, real-world compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques condense information from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable ones. Across vision, speech, recommendation, generative models, and natural language processing, practitioners use a mix of logit-based soft-label supervision, feature imitation, data distillation, multi-teacher fusion, curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware search to trade accuracy for latency, memory, or interpretability. Empirical work shows distilled students can often approach teacher accuracy while enabling deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings; theoretical and empirical analyses attribute much of KD’s effectiveness to the regularizing properties of soft targets, while recent extensions explicitly address adversarial robustness, decision-boundary transfer, domain adaptation, continual learning, and task-specific constraints. Remaining challenges include preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors (e.g., low-frequency phenomena), designing teacher-free or data-free alternatives, and building principled curricula and multi-source transfers that maximize student utility in downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies aim to transfer predictive behavior from larger or more expensive models to smaller, faster, or more resource-efficient ones. The literature shows a variety of mechanisms (soft-label supervision, intermediate-feature alignment, progressive module replacement, adversarial feature matching), data- and training-focused interventions (data selection, augmentation, mixup, control of dataset complexity), and hybrid combinations with pruning or ensembling. Empirical results across NLP and vision tasks indicate that KD can preserve much of teacher performance while accelerating inference, but success depends strongly on (a) the choice of distillation targets and layer mappings, (b) the complexity and provenance of the distillation data, and (c) complementary techniques such as pre-training, feature-level matching, or structured pruning. Practical approaches therefore tailor the distillation recipe to model capacity, task characteristics, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ware
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical System for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and practical approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a system—covering teacher design, the training signal, data and augmentation, and efficiency constraints—KD can retain much of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and domain requirements. However, its success depends on careful choices about teacher quality, distillation objectives, available data, and complementary compression techniques; awareness of these factors yields the most reliable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: Practical Knowledge Distillation for Deploying Large NLP and Deep Models: A Unified Argument for Multi-Teacher, Data-Agnostic, and Federated Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and essential set of techniques for compressing large deep and language models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. A mature KD strategy must simultaneously preserve teacher knowledge, generalize across domains and distributions, and respect deployment constraints (e.g., lack of original data or heterogeneous client devices). Empirical and methodological advances show that combining multi-teacher strategies, data-agnostic/distillation-from-generator approaches, feature-level projectors or ensembles, targeted augmentation, and adaptations for federated settings yields robust, efficient student models that approach teacher performance while meeting real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide a broad, practically oriented toolkit for shrinking large neural models while retaining most of their performance. Methods include transferring soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, adapting teacher or student architectures, using adversarial or data-free sample generation, and combining distillation with quantization or pruning. Empirical results across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks show substantial latency and memory gains; success depends on what signals are transferred, how layers are matched, data availability and augmentation, and the deployment constraints that shape algorithmic choices.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression and Practical NLP Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teacher's effectiveness. A growing body of work shows KD's versatility across modalities (vision, speech, text), deployment regimes (edge devices, distributed training), and model families (transformers, convolutional nets, generative models). Combining richer teacher signals (intermediate representations, attention maps, or learned teacher updates), stronger input-side practices (data augmentation), and complementary compression methods (architecture search, pruning) yields robust, efficient students suitable for real-world constraints. This paper argues that distillation should be treated not as a single recipe but as a flexible toolkit whose components are chosen to match task constraints, and it highlights promising techniques to improve transfer fidelity, training efficiency, and downstream performance.
