papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation unifies multiple strategies for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable models while preserving performance. It supports a range of goals — parameter and latency reduction, robustness, interpretability, and privacy-aware deployment — by transferring information from a teacher to a student via soft outputs, intermediate representations, or structural/architectural guidance. Practical and research advances show that combining distillation modes (feature-level, output-level, progressive module replacement), data augmentation, and adaptive teacher training yields compact models that approach teacher performance even under limited data, heterogeneous devices, or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Figueroa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies condense large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or lower-precision students suitable for deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Research has produced a taxonomy of approaches—soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate/feature imitation, relational or attention-based losses, multi-teacher fusion, data-free and zero-shot protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates that properly designed distillation pipelines can preserve most teacher performance across vision and language tasks while enabling substantial gains in inference speed and memory; theoretical analyses attribute much of KD’s benefit to regularization from soft targets and the transfer of inductive biases. Remaining challenges include handling teacher–student capacity mismatch, preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors, operating without original training data, and designing adaptive, task-aware distillation signals.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are widely used to transfer behavior from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling deployment under resource constraints. Research over the past decade has developed variants that target outputs (soft labels), internal representations (layer-wise and attention-based methods), data regimes (data-free or distilled training sets), and architecture search for task-aware compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both the practical gains and fundamental limits of distillation, and points to best practices such as pre-training compact models, selecting or synthesizing appropriate training data, and aligning student capacity to distilled signal.

papers_seen.author: Pope
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) condenses the functionality of larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. Across vision and NLP, KD variants—logit/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, online and multi-teacher schemes, and task-adaptive architecture search—have enabled deployment of compact models with strong empirical performance while revealing trade-offs in teacher–student alignment, data availability, and robustness. Key open challenges include principled teacher selection and weighting, effective data-free distillation, and preserving fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors during compression.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic for transferring soft targets into a unifying toolkit that enables model compression, deployment on constrained devices, privacy-aware release, and modality transfer. By combining architectural mapping, contrastive and adversarial objectives, and data-free or federated setups, KD can preserve much of a teacher model's performance while drastically reducing footprint and computation. This makes KD essential for translating state-of-the-art large models into real-world, resource-limited, and privacy-sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques reduce model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger or more informed models to smaller ones. Methods vary from soft-label supervision and layer mapping to data-free generation, adversarial sample selection, federated and privacy-preserving protocols, and task- or domain-aware adaptation. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, and generative modeling show that distillation can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, but performance depends sensitively on what information is transferred, how samples are selected, and whether pretraining or task adaptation is used. Practical use favors hybrids that combine architectural search, selective or weighted distillation, and generation or rehearsal strategies when original data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Multifaceted Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a single training trick but a central, practical framework for compressing large models into deployable students. When treated as a toolbox—combining soft-label transfer, representation-level alignment, data augmentation or synthesis, and integration with other compression methods—KD enables substantial reductions in memory and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. However, realizing those gains requires deliberate design: choosing which teacher signals to transfer, addressing optimization and capacity mismatches, and using data-aware or data-free strategies when original training data are unavailable. I argue that KD should be the core component of any production-focused compression pipeline, paired with representation-level objectives and careful data strategies to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical path to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A range of KD mechanisms—including soft-target supervision, intermediate feature or attention matching, multi-teacher fusion, data-free synthesis, and input-side augmentation—enable tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, privacy, and robustness. KD works best when its components are selected and adapted to deployment constraints: student capacity, available (or private) data, domain shift, and adversarial threats. However, important limitations remain, including distributional mismatch between teacher and student inputs, the preservation of robustness and fairness properties, and principled teacher selection. This article argues that a hybrid, constraint-aware KD strategy that combines representation-level transfer, data augmentation, and robustness- or privacy-aware synthesis offers the most reliable route to practical compression in real-world NLP and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD operates through multiple mechanisms—matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, transferring relational structure, and providing regularization—that together enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. KD integrates naturally with other compression methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization), supports data-free and privacy-sensitive settings, and scales across modalities and deployment constraints. At the same time, effective distillation requires careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to map teacher and student layers, how to handle imperfect teachers and data mismatch, and when to combine KD with complementary techniques. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a toolbox rather than a single recipe and offers practical, evidence-based recommendations for deploying KD in real systems.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. Research over the past decade has produced a wide array of distillation variants (logit-based supervision, feature and attention matching, multi- and self-distillation, data-free methods) and shown how KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet practical constraints. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both the strengths of KD (regularization, practical deployment gains, domain adaptation) and its limits (optimization difficulty, capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors), motivating a pragmatic set of design choices for robust compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: The Central, Practical, and Conditional Role of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible set of techniques for transferring useful behavior from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can meet deployment constraints while retaining much of the teacher’s utility. KD methods span soft-target matching, intermediate representation and layer-wise alignment, ensemble-to-single transfers, task-adaptive architecture search, and data-free or privacy-conscious pipelines. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that approach teacher performance across NLP, speech, and vision tasks, and that combining KD with architecture-aware compression or augmentation strategies often yields the best trade-offs. However, KD has limits: student capacity, the availability and quality of distilled data, and inherited teacher biases can all constrain outcomes. Responsible and effective compression therefore requires selecting the appropriate distillation signals, considering task and deployment constraints, and combining KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or fairness-aware objectives).

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression approaches transform large, high-performance neural models into smaller, faster models suitable for constrained deployment while attempting to preserve task performance. Methods range from transferring softened output distributions to matching intermediate representations, designing task-aware layer mappings, synthesizing or augmenting data for training, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications include compressing pretrained transformers for NLP, improving robustness under domain shift, enabling on-device inference and federated learning with heterogeneous devices, and training non-autoregressive sequence models. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both practical gains and limitations: distillation can yield compact models with strong accuracy but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, availability or synthesis of data, and handling low-frequency or domain-specific phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression strategies have become central for deploying high-performing deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Research has developed a spectrum of techniques — from soft-target supervision and intermediate-layer transfer to multi-teacher, data-free, and federated variants — and combined distillation with pruning and architecture search to compress large transformers and other architectures. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both practical gains (speed, memory, privacy) and fundamental tradeoffs (bias–variance, data heterogeneity, and information loss), pointing to hybrid protocols and adaptive selection of distillation signals as promising directions.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models so that compact models can retain much of the performance of their teachers. Across modalities and tasks, KD has evolved from simple soft-target (logit) matching to include feature- and layer-level supervision, online and multi-teacher schemes, meta-learned teachers, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with quantization and low-precision inference. Empirical work shows KD can substantially reduce model size and inference cost with modest performance loss, but success depends on careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student representations, and how to handle limited or mismatched data. Remaining practical issues include teacher–student heterogeneity, propagation of teacher errors, robustness to domain shifts, and limits to compression for some generative and structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural networks so they can run efficiently in production and on resource-constrained devices. Recent work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and that a range of complementary techniques—data augmentation, multi-teacher schedules, internal representation matching, layer alignment, meta-learning of teachers, and robustness-aware objectives—meaningfully improve student quality or transfer desirable properties. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on optimization, the choice of teacher/student architectures, and the distributional complexity of the training data. I argue that best practice for KD in deep learning and NLP is to treat it as a family of methods to be combined—augmenting data, distilling intermediate representations, leveraging multiple or adaptive teachers, and explicitly distilling robustness—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression methods form a diverse toolkit for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of the performance of larger teachers. Research spans soft-label and self-distillation strategies, layer- and representation-level transfers, architecture-aware and task-adaptive compression, and deployment-aware approaches that combine pruning, quantization, and distillation. Empirical work shows that careful choice of distillation signal (logits, intermediate representations, or feature maps), alignment strategy between teacher and student layers, data augmentation, and optimization scheduling materially affects student performance. Practical systems exploit these design choices to compress large pre-trained language models, accelerate inference, enable heterogeneous-device training, or improve low-precision networks. Despite progress, open questions remain about principled objective design, sample efficiency under limited data, and theory connecting transferred representations to generalization.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Practical Prescriptions for Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students suitable for deployment. While KD reliably reduces model size and inference cost, its effectiveness depends critically on choices around teacher design, the training signal (soft labels vs. representations), the data used for distillation, and additional constraints such as fairness and privacy. To realize reliable, high-quality compressed models in NLP and related domains, practitioners should treat KD as a system composed of complementary ingredients—data augmentation, multi-teacher or meta-learned teachers, representation-level objectives, and interventions for bias and privacy—rather than a single off-the-shelf loss.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. Its effectiveness depends not only on transferring final outputs but also on choosing what knowledge to transfer (samples, internal representations, or layers), preparing students (pre-training or architecture search), and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, low-precision arithmetic). However, distillation is not a panacea: optimization difficulties and imperfect teachers can limit how closely students match teachers and how much generalization benefit is obtained. Careful, task-aware design and hybrid pipelines produce the most reliable gains.

papers_seen.author: Archer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can preserve predictive performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its strengths derive from a variety of mechanisms — soft-label matching, internal-feature alignment, layer-mapping, and task-adaptive architecture design — and from being combinable with complementary compression techniques. However, realizing consistent gains requires careful choice of distilled targets, attention to representation alignment between teacher and student, and explicit handling of data-, fairness-, and robustness-related risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a toolbox of targeted interventions rather than a single recipe, and provides concise, evidence-based recommendations for practitioners compressing models in vision and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques enable deployment of large deep models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students, combining approaches such as soft‑label supervision, layer-wise or representation matching, and architectural reduction (pruning, layer skipping, parameter sharing). Research has extended distillation beyond supervised classification to domains including language models, sequence tasks, generative models, federated settings, domain adaptation, and few-shot or data-scarce regimes. Key practical challenges include maintaining accuracy under dataset or domain shift, training without access to original data, handling heterogeneous compute across devices, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and improving training efficiency. Effective solutions mix algorithmic choices (loss design, example selection, curriculum), data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or distilled data), and system-level integrations (joint optimization with pruning or layer removal).

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used technique to transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. It serves both model compression and training-stabilization roles across vision, speech, and language tasks. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online/co-distillation among peers, feature- and representation-level matching, and hybrid schemes that combine distillation with quantization or specialized training objectives. Empirical evidence shows KD can improve accuracy, generalization, robustness, and inference efficiency, but its success depends on data complexity, teacher design, and the type of knowledge transferred.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or transfers knowledge from large, often expensive teacher models into smaller or more efficient student models. Research has developed diverse KD mechanisms — soft-label distillation, intermediate feature matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data-centric augmentations — and applied them across domains (vision, multimodal, language, graph, and generative models). Empirical work demonstrates KD can retain much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and theoretical and empirical analyses link KD to regularization effects (e.g., label smoothing and bias–variance tradeoffs). Practical adaptations address modality misalignment, low-resource data, robustness to adversaries, and task-specific compression. Remaining challenges include principled teacher selection, distributional mismatch between distilled and original data, and scaling KD to large multimodal and structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool to make large deep models practical: it reduces model size and latency, enables domain adaptation, preserves privacy and scalability, and can even improve robustness when applied carefully. Successful deployments balance which teacher signals are transferred (logits, features, attention or answers), how they are aligned (layer-wise, projector-mediated, task-aware filters), and the training setup (multi-teacher, online, or adversarial). I argue that a principled combination of feature-level guidance, task-aware selection, and appropriate distillation architecture gives the best tradeoffs for NLP deployment: it preserves downstream performance while enabling orders-of-magnitude gains in speed, capacity, and deployability.

papers_seen.author: Deleon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transform large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or more private students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structured signals. Over the past decade these methods have evolved from logits-based soft-label transfer to a wide range of strategies including feature- and attention-matching, layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, data-free and privacy-preserving protocols, and adaptations for few-shot or federated settings. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation pipelines can retain much of teacher performance while substantially reducing model size and inference cost; however, effectiveness depends on what is distilled, student capacity, data availability, and practical constraints such as privacy, communication, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression across Modalities and Deployment Constraints
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from a teacher to a student, KD can preserve accuracy while reducing model size and inference cost. Combining KD with task-aware objectives, data-augmentation strategies, and data-free synthesis techniques further extends its applicability to settings with limited task data, privacy constraints, or strict latency requirements. This paper argues that a principled, hybrid KD approach—tailored to the modality and deployment constraints—offers the best path to deployable, high-quality compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Multi-Tool Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single recipe but as a flexible family of methods that, when combined with task-aware design and complementary compression techniques, enables deployment of compact models with strong utility. KD can transfer final-output behavior, intermediate representations, and structured relationships; it can operate with or without original training data, be adapted for privacy-sensitive or federated settings, and be combined with quantization or pruning to meet hardware constraints. Effective practice requires attention to what is distilled, how teachers and students are prepared, and how KD is integrated into the broader compression pipeline to avoid propagation of teacher biases or degradation on rare or shifted data.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Mckee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Partial Solution for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile means to compress large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their teacher performance. In practice KD enables latency- and memory-constrained deployment, supports continual and domain adaptation, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search to meet engineering constraints. However, KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with low-frequency or fine-grained behaviors, and requires task-aware alignment of signals and data strategies (including privacy-preserving or data-free approaches) to realize consistent benefits. I argue KD should be treated as a flexible toolkit that is integrated with task-aware layer mapping, privacy and data strategies, and complementary compression methods to produce robust, high-utility compressed models for NLP and other domains.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structured relationships. Across deep learning and NLP, KD enables deployment of performant models under latency, memory, and privacy constraints and is routinely combined with complementary compression methods. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer (logits vs. features), how to align teacher and student architectures, the availability and design of distillation data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and training protocols that mitigate capacity and distribution mismatches. Open challenges include robust teacher selection, data- and domain-mismatch, and scaling distillation methods to heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for NLP: Efficacy, Best Practices, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in NLP. When applied with attention to what to transfer (logits, features, or layers), how to align teacher and student representations, and how to prepare data and student initialization, KD yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance. However, distillation can propagate teacher errors, suffer from representation mismatch, and interact with privacy and robustness requirements—so practitioners must combine KD with complementary techniques and careful validation to meet real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation in NLP: Pre-training, Task-Awareness, Privacy, and Robustness
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large language models into smaller, faster students for NLP applications. Its effectiveness depends not only on the student-teacher framework but on complementary practices: pre-training compact models, aligning distilled signals to task-relevant representations, handling limited or private data, leveraging multiple teachers when available, and explicitly distilling for robustness. When these elements are combined and tuned, distillation yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) remains a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across tasks and modalities. KD's benefits arise from multiple mechanisms: transferring soft output distributions, mimicking intermediate features, providing regularization that improves generalization, and enabling compression even when original training data are unavailable. Empirically and theoretically, KD should be treated as a toolbox: select loss forms (logit, feature, relational), augment or synthesize data when needed, and consider joint training of teacher and student or teacher design that is friendly to students. Combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, pruning, architecture design), KD helps produce efficient models that retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting real deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while trying to retain their performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher output distributions to transferring internal representations or structured feature information, and from single-stage offline distillation to online and multi-teacher schemes. Empirical work across natural language, speech, vision and multimodal tasks shows that careful design—such as aligning intermediate features, adapting teachers to be student-friendly, using task- and domain-aware distillation, and leveraging online or instance-aware teacher weighting—can substantially reduce model size and latency with small performance loss. Still, distillation can introduce task-specific failure modes (e.g., degraded rare-word behavior or overfitting to teacher feature statistics), and practical deployment requires addressing teacher–student heterogeneity, data availability, and scalability.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Multifaceted Tool for Efficient and Responsible Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single compression trick: it is a flexible toolkit for producing compact, fast, and often more deployable models while enabling privacy-preserving, domain-adaptive, and robustness-improving workflows. When combined with complementary practices—pre-training compact architectures, matching intermediate representations, selecting or synthesizing appropriate distillation data, multi-stage or multi-teacher schedules, and privacy-aware procedures—KD yields practical students that approach teacher performance under real-world constraints. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher–student alignment, data provenance, and explicit choices about what knowledge to transfer; these limitations motivate principled distillation design rather than off-the-shelf application.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques reduce model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger or more informed models to smaller ones. Methods vary from soft-label supervision and layer mapping to data-free generation, adversarial sample selection, federated and privacy-preserving protocols, and task- or domain-aware adaptation. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, and generative modeling show that distillation can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices, but performance depends sensitively on what information is transferred, how samples are selected, and whether pretraining or task adaptation is used. Practical use favors hybrids that combine architectural search, selective or weighted distillation, and generation or rehearsal strategies when original data are unavailable.
