papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Frost
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable means to compress large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. When matched to task constraints—choosing what teacher signals to transfer, how to align layers or features, and whether or how to handle missing or private training data—KD enables deployment of competitive models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: careful design (task-aware layer selection, many-to-many mapping for large pre-trained transformers, selective sample weighting, and data-free procedures when needed) is required to avoid propagating teacher errors, worsening robustness, or underfitting compact students. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central compression engine for modern deep learning and NLP pipelines, but that success depends on matching KD mechanisms to application constraints and combining KD with complementary engineering (efficient distillation pipelines and synthetic-data or adversarial generators when data are unavailable).

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Conditional Endorsement
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques are indispensable tools for deploying high-capacity deep models in resource- and latency-constrained settings. When combined with architecture-aware strategies, task adaptation, and data-aware protocols, KD recovers much of teacher performance while enabling substantial speed and size reductions. However, distillation is not a universal remedy: optimization difficulties, domain and low-frequency token mismatches, privacy or data-availability constraints, and fairness concerns require tailored remedies. Effective compression thus integrates KD with architecture search, progressive replacement, data-free methods, and fairness- and federated-aware training to achieve reliable, deployable students.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical toolkit to transfer performance and representational structure from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under memory, compute, or latency constraints. Research has expanded KD beyond simple soft-label matching to encompass intermediate-feature imitation, many-to-many layer mapping, relational and task-aware transfers, multi-teacher fusion, and input-side interventions (e.g., data augmentation or synthesized inputs). Empirical work shows distilled students frequently approach teacher performance when methods are matched to the task and architecture, but significant open problems remain around robustness, low-frequency behavior, teacher errors, and data- or privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. Methods include soft-target or logit matching, feature- and layer-level mimicry, multi-teacher and ensemble-driven transfer, data-free or zero-shot approaches, and combinations with pruning or quantization. Distillation works both as a mechanism for transmitting ‘‘dark knowledge’’ about class relationships and as a regularizer that can improve student generalization, but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, data or synthetic inputs, teacher design, and alignment between teacher and student. Practical goals—reducing inference cost, enabling edge deployment, preserving accuracy under domain shift, and meeting privacy or fairness constraints—are achievable in many settings but require task- and data-aware design. Open problems include robust, privacy-preserving distillation without teacher data, principled teacher selection and weighting, theoretical understanding of optimization gaps, and balancing compression with fairness and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Practical Pathways for Compressing Large NLP Models: Pre-train the Student, Distill Carefully, and Guard for Data & Robustness
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach to compress large deep learning models for NLP and related tasks. When the student model is itself pre-trained, distillation yields especially strong and consistent gains; complementary methods — including data augmentation during distillation, progressive module replacement, ensemble teachers or teacher adaptation, and data-free or privacy-aware distillation — address common deployment constraints such as limited task data, inference cost, data access, and adversarial robustness. Combining these techniques and choosing distillation targets and schedules with theoretical and empirical guidance yields compact models that retain much of the original performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques shrink large neural models into smaller, faster models for constrained deployment while attempting to preserve task performance. A diverse set of approaches—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or generative sample synthesis—has emerged across vision, language, multimodal, and graph tasks. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention maps, or structural priors), how to align heterogeneous architectures, whether teacher or student are adapted during training, and how to handle limited or absent training data. Empirical work shows substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost are possible with modest performance loss, but open problems remain around principled teacher selection, robustness under domain shift, privacy, and closing optimization/capacity gaps between teachers and students.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical but Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones. When used thoughtfully, KD can preserve much of a teacher's performance while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on which signals are transferred (logits, features, relational information), alignment between teacher and student, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and awareness of teacher imperfections. Combining KD with representation-level matching, task-aware layer alignment, online or federated protocols, and data strategies yields the best trade-offs for real systems.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a logits-matching trick into a broad set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from large neural teachers. Modern KD variants transfer soft predictions, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structure; they are combined with data-centric practices (augmentation, synthetic and zero-shot data) and complementary compression (pruning, architecture search) to meet real-world latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work demonstrates strong gains in NLP (notably transformer compression) as well as vision, graphs, and federated settings, while theoretical and empirical studies reveal optimization challenges, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional/heterogeneity limitations. Practical pipelines favor pretraining or progressive replacement, representation-level matching, task-adaptive data strategies, and awareness of privacy and robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. Its effectiveness depends not only on transferring final outputs but also on choosing what knowledge to transfer (samples, internal representations, or layers), preparing students (pre-training or architecture search), and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, low-precision arithmetic). However, distillation is not a panacea: optimization difficulties and imperfect teachers can limit how closely students match teachers and how much generalization benefit is obtained. Careful, task-aware design and hybrid pipelines produce the most reliable gains.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—language understanding, machine translation, reading comprehension, and large-scale distributed training—recent work shows KD can improve inference speed, aid domain adaptation, enable training without original data, and increase robustness. Combining innovations in layer mapping, feature-level transfer, online and data-free techniques, and teacher optimization yields the best trade-offs for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Archer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can preserve predictive performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its strengths derive from a variety of mechanisms — soft-label matching, internal-feature alignment, layer-mapping, and task-adaptive architecture design — and from being combinable with complementary compression techniques. However, realizing consistent gains requires careful choice of distilled targets, attention to representation alignment between teacher and student, and explicit handling of data-, fairness-, and robustness-related risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a toolbox of targeted interventions rather than a single recipe, and provides concise, evidence-based recommendations for practitioners compressing models in vision and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Composable Toolkit for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a composable toolkit—combining soft-target transfer, representation-level matching, data augmentation, selective sample strategies, and multi-teacher or federated adaptations—KD can produce efficient models that preserve much of teacher performance while meeting deployment constraints. However, KD has known failure modes (teacher error propagation, data- and device-heterogeneity, and sample-wise regularization effects) that require explicit remedies and system-level design choices to ensure robust transfer.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Practical, Task-Aware, and Privacy-Conscious Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical suite of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment across modalities and tasks. Effective KD goes beyond naive logits matching: task-aware layer-wise alignment, progressive module replacement, multi-teacher schedules, and architecture-aware search can preserve accuracy while reducing compute and memory. Moreover, self-distillation and teacher-free variants reduce dependence on strong teachers, and specialized KD variants address scarce data, privacy, and federated constraints. These directions together form a roadmap for applying KD in real-world deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Hancock
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single recipe for copying teacher logits into a central, flexible paradigm for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and behaviors of larger teachers. KD methods vary in what they transfer (soft labels, intermediate features, relational structure), how they handle data availability (data-rich, data-free, federated), and how they combine with other compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical deployments select and tune KD components to match modality, data-privacy constraints, and latency or memory budgets.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Variants
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks, a consistent set of practices has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, intermediate-layer matching, and task- or domain-specific adaptation—augmented by variants that address missing data, distributed training, privacy, and teacher-student mismatch. Empirical results show that distilled students can approach teacher accuracy while enjoying large gains in inference speed and memory, and recent work clarifies when and why distillation acts as an effective regularizer.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Remaining Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, flexible strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in parameters and latency, and it generalizes across settings from data-poor or privacy-sensitive deployments to multi-teacher and online training regimes. However, practical success depends on careful choice of what to transfer (logits, features, relations), handling limited or absent training data, mitigating transferred biases, and aligning teacher-student architectures. I argue that KD should be the primary tool in production compression pipelines but must be combined with data synthesis, teacher selection/calibration, and fairness-aware design to realize robust, reliable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transform large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable ones by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural properties from teacher to student. Approaches vary from logits-based transfer to feature- or module-level imitation, multi-teacher and meta-learned schemes, data-free (zero-shot) methods, and procedures designed for robustness or computational efficiency. Across vision, speech, graph, and NLP settings (including large pretrained Transformer models), distillation has enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of the original performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer (probabilities, features, modules), how to generate or augment data for transfer, and how to preserve or transfer robustness and task-specific inductive biases. Remaining challenges include matching teacher performance across tasks with minimal data, ensuring robustness under adversarial or distributional shift, and balancing efficiency with fidelity in large-scale pretrained language models.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a diverse toolkit for transferring information from larger, more expensive models to smaller, faster, or more constrained models. Methods range from matching output distributions to aligning intermediate representations, altering training curricula, and designing compression-aware teachers or architectures. These approaches have been applied across domains including vision, speech, translation, retrieval, and on-device deployment, and have been adapted to privacy- and communication-constrained settings. Empirical and analytical work has clarified different mechanisms by which distillation aids learning, and recent work explores automation, adversarial feature transfer, sample selection, and architecture-aware strategies to improve efficiency without sacrificing much performance.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Integrated Feature-, Data- and Robustness-aware Knowledge Distillation for Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from simple logit matching into a toolbox of complementary techniques. Empirical and theoretical work shows that (1) matching internal features often transfers richer representations than logits alone, (2) the choice of input-side interventions (e.g., data augmentation) substantially changes distillation dynamics, and (3) robustness, teacher quality, and sample selection must be addressed explicitly. I argue that effective model compression in deep learning and NLP requires integrating feature-level mimicry with careful input-space design, selective or confidence-weighted teacher signals, and robustness-aware objectives. This combined approach maximizes student performance while keeping models compact and deployment-ready.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Best Practices and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable models across vision, language, and structured-data domains. KD works at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention, and structural guidance) and combines naturally with complementary methods—student pretraining, data augmentation or synthesis, multi-teacher and ensemble signals, architecture-aware losses, and privacy-aware generation—to produce compact models that retain much of the teacher’s utility while satisfying latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Effective deployment requires careful choices of distillation targets, alignment strategies, and data-handling procedures, and awareness of common failure modes (optimization instability, teacher error propagation, and domain/device heterogeneity).

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a logits-matching trick into a broad set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from large neural teachers. Modern KD variants transfer soft predictions, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structure; they are combined with data-centric practices (augmentation, synthetic and zero-shot data) and complementary compression (pruning, architecture search) to meet real-world latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work demonstrates strong gains in NLP (notably transformer compression) as well as vision, graphs, and federated settings, while theoretical and empirical studies reveal optimization challenges, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional/heterogeneity limitations. Practical pipelines favor pretraining or progressive replacement, representation-level matching, task-adaptive data strategies, and awareness of privacy and robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression approaches transform large, high-performance neural models into smaller, faster models suitable for constrained deployment while attempting to preserve task performance. Methods range from transferring softened output distributions to matching intermediate representations, designing task-aware layer mappings, synthesizing or augmenting data for training, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Applications include compressing pretrained transformers for NLP, improving robustness under domain shift, enabling on-device inference and federated learning with heterogeneous devices, and training non-autoregressive sequence models. Empirical and theoretical work highlights both practical gains and limitations: distillation can yield compact models with strong accuracy but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, availability or synthesis of data, and handling low-frequency or domain-specific phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Farrell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Strategy for Model Compression across Modalities and Deployment Constraints
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible paradigm for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from a teacher to a student, KD can preserve accuracy while reducing model size and inference cost. Combining KD with task-aware objectives, data-augmentation strategies, and data-free synthesis techniques further extends its applicability to settings with limited task data, privacy constraints, or strict latency requirements. This paper argues that a principled, hybrid KD approach—tailored to the modality and deployment constraints—offers the best path to deployable, high-quality compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques condense information from larger or more complex models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable ones. Across vision, speech, recommendation, generative models, and natural language processing, practitioners use a mix of logit-based soft-label supervision, feature imitation, data distillation, multi-teacher fusion, curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware search to trade accuracy for latency, memory, or interpretability. Empirical work shows distilled students can often approach teacher accuracy while enabling deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings; theoretical and empirical analyses attribute much of KD’s effectiveness to the regularizing properties of soft targets, while recent extensions explicitly address adversarial robustness, decision-boundary transfer, domain adaptation, continual learning, and task-specific constraints. Remaining challenges include preserving robustness and fine-grained behaviors (e.g., low-frequency phenomena), designing teacher-free or data-free alternatives, and building principled curricula and multi-source transfers that maximize student utility in downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool Beyond Simple Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be understood and applied as a flexible toolbox rather than merely a compression trick. KD enables compression, regularization, privacy-preserving transfer, and adaptation across diverse constraints (data scarcity, heterogeneous devices, federated settings). Effective practice combines soft-target supervision with representation-level alignment, architecture-aware methods (pruning, quantization, search), and privacy-aware or teacher-free variants. However, careful design is required to avoid capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors, and robustness or bias degradation.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger or ensembles of models to smaller, more efficient models. Across computer vision, natural language processing, and generative modeling, research has developed many variants: prediction-level soft-target transfer, layer- and representation-level supervision, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and data-free distillation, and privacy-preserving compression. Empirical work shows that these approaches can substantially reduce model size and inference cost with modest loss in task performance, but practical success depends on alignment between teacher and student capacity, careful choice of what and how to transfer, and the availability (or absence) of original training data. Theoretical and empirical analyses highlight optimization and capacity gaps that limit perfect imitation, motivate task-aware and attention-guided transfers, and point to trade-offs when teachers are imperfect. Remaining challenges include principled teacher selection and weighting, robust data-free distillation, and reconciling compression with privacy and fairness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practical Trade-offs, and Empirical Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques seek to transfer predictive power and internal knowledge from large, expensive models (teachers) into smaller, faster models (students), enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Approaches vary from matching teacher output distributions to transferring intermediate representations, designing many-to-many layer mappings, performing data-free distillation when original training data are unavailable, and distilling ensembles or multiple teachers into a single model. In NLP, these methods are applied to compress pre-trained language models, speed up evaluation metrics, and produce task-adaptive compressed models while attempting to retain generalization and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Practical and Principled Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central tool for compressing large neural networks so they can run efficiently in production and on resource-constrained devices. Recent work shows KD can preserve much of the teacher performance while reducing inference cost, and that a range of complementary techniques—data augmentation, multi-teacher schedules, internal representation matching, layer alignment, meta-learning of teachers, and robustness-aware objectives—meaningfully improve student quality or transfer desirable properties. At the same time, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on optimization, the choice of teacher/student architectures, and the distributional complexity of the training data. I argue that best practice for KD in deep learning and NLP is to treat it as a family of methods to be combined—augmenting data, distilling intermediate representations, leveraging multiple or adaptive teachers, and explicitly distilling robustness—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques aim to transfer predictive behavior from large, expensive models to smaller, faster models so they can be deployed under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Over the past decade research has produced a taxonomy of distillation mechanisms (logit/soft-target matching, representation or feature imitation, multi-teacher and ensemble-to-student transfers), adaptations for low-data or data-free settings, and combinations of distillation with architecture search and pruning. Empirical work shows that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance at large computational savings, but also highlights practical failure modes: students often do not perfectly match teacher predictive distributions, optimization choices and training data matter strongly, and specialized methods are needed for task-specific or distributed scenarios. Recent advances emphasize multi-stage/multi-teacher schedules, augmentation-aware objectives, online distributed training, and loss formulations that better capture teacher uncertainty; combining these approaches with automated architecture search and structured pruning yields stronger, hardware-aware compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Multifaceted Strategy for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large deep and NLP models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. Beyond matching final outputs, modern KD variants transfer intermediate representations, adapt teacher behavior to students, and operate when task data are limited or unavailable. KD is most effective when combined with task-aware signal selection, teacher design, data strategies, and complementary compression such as architecture search or pruning; used in this way, KD enables compact models that approach teacher performance while addressing real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones while trying to retain their performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher output distributions to transferring internal representations or structured feature information, and from single-stage offline distillation to online and multi-teacher schemes. Empirical work across natural language, speech, vision and multimodal tasks shows that careful design—such as aligning intermediate features, adapting teachers to be student-friendly, using task- and domain-aware distillation, and leveraging online or instance-aware teacher weighting—can substantially reduce model size and latency with small performance loss. Still, distillation can introduce task-specific failure modes (e.g., degraded rare-word behavior or overfitting to teacher feature statistics), and practical deployment requires addressing teacher–student heterogeneity, data availability, and scalability.

papers_seen.author: Frost
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable means to compress large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. When matched to task constraints—choosing what teacher signals to transfer, how to align layers or features, and whether or how to handle missing or private training data—KD enables deployment of competitive models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: careful design (task-aware layer selection, many-to-many mapping for large pre-trained transformers, selective sample weighting, and data-free procedures when needed) is required to avoid propagating teacher errors, worsening robustness, or underfitting compact students. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the central compression engine for modern deep learning and NLP pipelines, but that success depends on matching KD mechanisms to application constraints and combining KD with complementary engineering (efficient distillation pipelines and synthetic-data or adversarial generators when data are unavailable).

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used technique to transfer information from larger or more complex models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. It serves both model compression and training-stabilization roles across vision, speech, and language tasks. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online/co-distillation among peers, feature- and representation-level matching, and hybrid schemes that combine distillation with quantization or specialized training objectives. Empirical evidence shows KD can improve accuracy, generalization, robustness, and inference efficiency, but its success depends on data complexity, teacher design, and the type of knowledge transferred.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compressing and Adapting Deep Models in NLP and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while preserving or even improving task performance. Across settings—domain adaptation, resource-constrained deployment, privacy-limited releases, sequence generation, and large-scale distributed training—distillation methods enable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and cost. By leveraging teacher signals (soft targets, feature representations, or ensembles), self-distillation, and data- or communication-efficient protocols, practitioners can tailor compression strategies to meet production constraints without wholesale redesign of model architectures.

papers_seen.author: Callahan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, widely applicable strategy for compressing large neural networks into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation enables deployment of powerful pretrained models in resource-constrained settings, supports specialization (e.g., task or domain adaptation), and can be combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, pruning, architecture search) to produce practical, production-ready models. Advances in distillation methodology — including multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, teacher meta-learning, and task-aware layer-wise alignment — address fundamental challenges of capacity mismatch, information selection, and optimization stability, leading to more robust and efficient student models. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of any production-focused compression pipeline for deep learning and NLP systems, and that research emphasis on better teacher–student dynamics and task-aware transfer will yield the largest practical gains.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large models and transferring their capabilities to smaller or specialized models. KD can operate at multiple levels (logits, intermediate layers, and features), can be combined with model pruning and precision reduction, and can support domain adaptation and on-device deployment. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on how teacher knowledge is represented and transferred, the choice of data and augmentations used during distillation, and the deployment context (e.g., heterogeneous federated environments). When methods for intermediate-layer alignment, feature mimicking, data-side regularization, and architecture-aware mapping are combined thoughtfully, KD yields compact, efficient models that retain much of the teacher’s performance while enabling practical deployment in resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Ortiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, mature toolkit for turning large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Approaches vary from transferring softened outputs to aligning intermediate representations or relational structure, from online and multi-teacher schemes to data-free and privacy-aware pipelines. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and other modalities shows that well-designed distillation can preserve most of a teacher's performance while delivering substantial reductions in inference cost, parameter count, and memory footprint. Practical success depends on matching distillation targets and schedules to student capacity and deployment constraints, handling limited or private data appropriately, and addressing robustness, fairness, and distribution-shift concerns.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and/or internal representations. A rich set of mechanisms—soft-target (logit) matching, feature or representation imitation, layer-wise mapping, multi-teacher and ensemble-to-student transfers, and data-free or privacy-aware strategies—has been developed and combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical evidence shows distilled students can recover much of teacher accuracy while substantially reducing latency and footprint, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, data and augmentation strategies, teacher quality, and training schedules. Ongoing work focuses on robustness to domain shift, heterogeneous devices, limited or unavailable data, and principled ways to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical path to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. A range of KD mechanisms—including soft-target supervision, intermediate feature or attention matching, multi-teacher fusion, data-free synthesis, and input-side augmentation—enable tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, privacy, and robustness. KD works best when its components are selected and adapted to deployment constraints: student capacity, available (or private) data, domain shift, and adversarial threats. However, important limitations remain, including distributional mismatch between teacher and student inputs, the preservation of robustness and fairness properties, and principled teacher selection. This article argues that a hybrid, constraint-aware KD strategy that combines representation-level transfer, data augmentation, and robustness- or privacy-aware synthesis offers the most reliable route to practical compression in real-world NLP and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Deep and NLP Models: Methods, Limits, and Complementary Techniques
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core strategy to compress large pre-trained deep models so they can be deployed in latency- and resource-constrained settings. KD variants—multi-teacher pipelines, layer-wise and task-aware alignment, self-distillation, and feature-level matching—enable small students to approach or match teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost. KD is most effective when combined with complementary approaches such as pruning and architecture search, and when adapted to domain or system constraints (e.g., federated or multi-device settings). However, KD is not a universal panacea: data heterogeneity, misaligned inputs between teacher and student, and inappropriate augmentation or feature transfer can limit gains, so careful design choices are required to realize practical compression.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile technique that enables compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' performance. When combined with complementary practices — pre-training compact architectures, aligning intermediate representations, data-centric augmentation, privacy-aware protocols, and task-aware loss design — distillation yields efficient models suitable for real-world NLP and multimodal deployments. However, KD is not a silver bullet: optimization difficulties, capacity mismatch, and data limitations require careful method choices and evaluation. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a central, pragmatic engine of model compression, but one that must be applied with principled, task-aware adjustments to achieve reliable gains in practice.
